He has had a long series of forgettable films over the years, and he may very well have more of them in future 😜 But Tara Singh reminds you what Sunny Deol is capable of when the character, dialogue and mass emotion align perfectly with his personality 🙏

The two iconic songs — Ghar Aaja Pardesi and Main Nikla Gaddi Leke — are retained, and they still carry almost the same magic they did 22 years ago 🙏🙏

If you watched GADAR back in 2001 and have memories attached to that era, GADAR 2 is a must-watch because it becomes a wonderful nostalgia trip into the period when massy patriotic Hindi films had their own unique theatrical flavour.

If you are a much younger viewer with no emotional connection to the original, though, you may want to keep your expectations in check. This filmmaking style belongs proudly to another era — and that is simultaneously its biggest strength and its biggest limitation.

e: BHOLA SHANKAR feels less like a movie and more like a చిరు ఉపాధి పధకం for people desperate to work with Chiranjeevi. The outdated remake, weak music, cringe comedy and wasted Vedalam moments convinced me that Chiru urgently needs fresher directors and content rather than another fan-driven project.
v: Don’t let regular reviews fool you — this Meher Ramesh remake is still better than the legendary Aacharyaaa 💪😂 That is also almost the nicest thing I can say about it.
body:
Don’t let the regular reviews fool you — Meher Ramesh’s remake is still better than Koratala Siva’s original masterpiece Aacharyaaa 💪😂

And that is probably the nicest thing I can say about BHOLA SHANKAR.

This doesn’t feel like a movie as much as a చిరు ఉపాధి పధకం — an employment scheme for people who desperately wanted to be part of a Chiranjeevi film 🙏

I strongly believe Chiru should stop entertaining so-called fans by automatically giving them opportunities in acting, direction or other departments simply because they belong to the bhajana batch.

This movie is a perfect example of how weak the final product can become when admiration for the star starts replacing honest creative collaboration.

Whatever the quality of a Chiranjeevi film, one thing that traditionally rarely disappoints is the music.

Well... thanks to Mahati Swara Sagar, BHOLA SHANKAR manages to disappoint me there too 😞

At times it feels as if the producers and Chiru himself wanted to put together a quick remake using an already outdated story, assuming familiarity and star power would do most of the work.

The project then seems to have attracted actors and technicians eager simply for the opportunity to say they worked with Megastar — which again brings me back to my చిరు ఉపాధి పధకం theory 😂

When this movie was announced, everybody was naturally sceptical. Still, I had one small hope: Vedalam had a couple of stylish, high-octane sequences that actually looked suitable for Meher Ramesh’s flashy filmmaking style.

Unfortunately, he manages to mess up even those opportunities.

I have always been a huge fan of Chiru’s comedy timing, but here the comedy felt cringe to the core.

The attempt to make Chiranjeevi imitate Pawan Kalyan looks artificial rather than affectionate, and the recreation of the famous nadumu scene from Kushi turns something cute and romantic in the original into something painfully awkward 🙄

It is high time Chiranjeevi works with new-age directors and newer content — even darker or more unusual subjects if needed — rather than repeatedly falling back on remakes that offer audiences almost nothing new.

More importantly, he should work with filmmakers who are confident enough to challenge him creatively, not people whose fandom automatically gives the star complete control over the content 😢

PS: Pawan Kalyan sudden ga women trafficking gurinchi maatladinappude telusukovalsindi... BHOLA SHANKAR promotions chesthunnadani 😉

e: JAILER is average-to-good as a film, but Nelson succeeds at something many recent directors struggled with: balancing Rajinikanth’s larger-than-life style with enough story to hold the movie together. The cameos and Anirudh’s terrific BGM provide most of the extra theatrical lift.
v: After a long time, a proper treat for Thalaivar fans — half-cooked story maybe, but Rajini’s swag + killer cameos + Anirudh BGM make it a far better Rajini outing than his recent run 🙏
body:
After a long time... this is a proper treat for Thalaivar fans!!!!

Nelson achieves something many new-age directors have struggled with: finding a reasonable balance between Rajinikanth’s style and a story without allowing the superstar treatment to completely swallow the movie.

Content-wise, the story is somewhere between half-cooked and decent and follows a structure that occasionally reminded me of the Vikram format, including its twists and extended-universe-style cameos.

But for a neutral viewer, what really holds the film together is Rajini’s swag.

Add the appearances by Shiva Rajkumar, Mohanlal and Jackie Shroff, then let Anirudh blast those moments with his terrific BGM... and suddenly even fairly ordinary material becomes a proper theatrical event.

Overall, JAILER is an Average-to-Good movie for me.

It definitely could have been better as a complete film, but it is still a far, far, far better Rajinikanth movie than most of what I had seen from him in the immediate years before this 🙏

t: Adipurush — My Take on the Reactions 😉
e: Five days after Adipurush released, I found the competing political theories around its failure more baffling than the film itself. My take was simpler: Ramayana deserved a modern retelling, the producer-director-star choices were understandable on paper, but the CGI, adaptation choices and execution went badly wrong.
v: Adipurush was badly made — but I still don’t buy the grand political conspiracy theories from either side. Sometimes a badly executed movie is simply... a badly executed movie 😉
body:
It had been almost five days since Adipurush released and, no doubt, I thought it was a badly made film.

But some of the grand theories being circulated online about why the movie was made — and who was supposedly behind it — baffled me even more than the movie itself 🤷🏻‍♂️

Opinion 1: “This was a political project built around Shri Ram sentiment.”

One side argued that a political party had effectively backed or taken ownership of the movie so that religious sentiment could be converted into money and political benefit.

My counter: I genuinely wondered whether people making that claim had watched the final product 😂 If an organised political machinery had carefully designed a religious propaganda film, I would at least expect the execution to be competent enough not to irritate even deeply religious viewers.

The final film, for me, was too badly handled to support the idea of some brilliantly coordinated political master plan.

Opinion 2: “This was an anti-Hindu Bollywood conspiracy.”

The opposite camp argued that Bollywood and political liberals had deliberately tried to damage Ramayana and portray Hindu culture badly.

My counter: I found that theory equally unconvincing. In the political climate of the time, deliberately spending enormous money on a nationally visible Ramayana adaptation purely to offend a massive audience would be an extraordinary commercial and political risk.

So what do I think actually happened?

Let’s start with the official producer, T-Series.

If we rewind to our childhood in the early and mid-1990s, many of us remember Gulshan Kumar and T-Series being strongly associated with devotional songs and religious content covering Hindu gods and goddesses.

So T-Series participating in a major Ramayana project never seemed strange to me, nor did I need a party-political explanation for it.

Also, if we look at Indian television and movie history, every generation or two has retold epics like Ramayana and Mahabharata using the storytelling styles and technology available at that time.

We have seen multiple television versions of Mahabharata — some hugely popular, some average and some forgettable.

But after the famous older Ramayana adaptations and the animated version many of us grew up with, a large-scale modern cinematic retelling of Ramayana had been due for a long time.

Maybe the cultural moment around the Ram Mandir construction made T-Series feel this was a particularly good time to attempt it. That possibility seems far more ordinary to me than either political conspiracy theory.

Then comes the director.

Om Raut had won significant recognition for Tanhaji, a large-scale historical film. On paper, I can understand why producers might have believed he could handle an epic project.

Once they decided to mount Ramayana at a huge scale, the budget naturally became enormous. To recover that investment, they needed a face with pan-India theatrical pull.

After Baahubali, choosing Prabhas as that face was commercially understandable — even if, in hindsight, whether he was the perfect fit for this particular role is a completely different question.

So far, so good.

For me, the major failure was the execution.

The team could not handle the level of CGI required convincingly, and they also seemed caught between faithfully retelling an epic and trying to redesign it for a modern audience that will question every creative shortcut.

They ultimately created their own heavily altered visual and tonal version of Ramayana — and many of those choices backfired badly.

That explanation may sound boring compared with a giant political conspiracy... but sometimes a badly planned and badly executed film is simply that.

And who am I to say all this?

I am neither here as a political devotee nor as a political hater. I am neither deeply religious nor an atheist. I am neither a hardcore Prabhas fan nor someone waiting to attack him.

I have loved and hated movies from every industry based primarily on what I experienced on screen, not on whatever political intent strangers online assign to them 😊

I am just an APOLITICAL MOVIE BUFF!!!!

e: My first Adipurush watch in Telugu 2D was overwhelmingly disappointing: bad dubbing, weak emotional connection, questionable casting and shockingly poor CGI. A later 3D rewatch improved the visual experience somewhat, but it could not fix the deeper problems in vision, character depth and execution.
v: Wonderful music trapped inside a badly executed epic — poor dubbing, misfit casting, artificial emotions and CGI that looked worse than TV serials in 2D 🤦‍♂️
body:
Recently, my friend Sandeep pointed out that many of my reviews seemed to begin with the same pattern — “Though I am not a big fan of...” 😂

He made me realise I had been repeating myself far too often. So thanks to him, I’m trying to change the writing style — and this review is officially dedicated to Sandeep 🙏🙏🙏

First, one important context: my initial Adipurush watch was the Telugu 2D version at Cinepolis. So my first reaction was based entirely on that experience.

NEGATIVES

  1. The Telugu dub was horrible. There were visible lip-sync issues even during Prabhas’s dialogues.
  2. I’m still not sure how the star cast was selected. At least for me, almost none of the major actors felt like the perfect fit for these iconic characters.
  3. Prabhas looked expressionless in many places, while Saif Ali Khan often went to the opposite extreme and felt over-expressive. Maybe acting against so much CGI contributed to that disconnect 🤷🏻‍♂️
  4. Yes, Ramayana is a story most of us already know. But if I judge this film as a standalone movie, there is hardly any point where the screenplay makes me emotionally connect with the characters on screen. The emotions often feel artificial because proper character depth is missing. The only reason we understand why everyone behaves the way they do is because we already know these characters from the epic.
  5. The CGI experience in 2D was HORRIBLE, to put it mildly. The demons in Omkar annayya’s old Mayadeepam episodes sometimes felt more convincing than what I was seeing in this massively expensive film 🤣
  6. Forget international standards — some of the graphics initially felt closer to Indian daily-soap quality 🤦‍♂️

POSITIVE

The one genuinely strong department for me was the BGM and songs 🙌

After watching Adipurush, my respect for Rajamouli multiplied several times over.

Simply having the intention to make something grand is never enough. To create actual grandeur on screen, you need vision, visualisation and execution — all three working together 🙏

I had previously criticised Gunasekhar for repeatedly attempting large period films such as Rudhramadevi and Shaakuntalam with below-par graphics.

After Adipurush, I genuinely felt Gunasekhar might have delivered a better Ramayana than Om Raut 😅

I decided to watch the film again in 3D that Sunday, hoping the format would at least change my opinion about the CGI 🤞

At the time, theatres were reserving a symbolic seat for Lord Hanuman. Looking at the 2D viewer experience, I joked that after the weekend they may need to reserve the entire theatre for Vanara Sainyam 🙏😂

UPDATE AFTER WATCHING IT AGAIN IN 3D

The 3D version is definitely far better at presenting whatever the team created.

The 2D presentation was simply horrible by comparison, and I genuinely wondered why they even released that version when it amplified so many of the visual weaknesses.

In 3D, the CGI experience at least moves closer to an average viewing experience.

Unfortunately, better presentation cannot repair the deeper issues: the casting, dubbing, lack of emotional depth and, most importantly, the confused execution of a story that deserved far more care.

e: As someone who gets scared even by Chandramukhi-level horror, I still walked into VIRUPAKSHA for the love of good cinema. The first half takes time to build its world, but the supernatural thriller elements, twists, technical craft and Samyuktha Menon’s performance make the second half genuinely rewarding.
v: A proper supernatural THRILLER with a slow-burn first half and a terrific second-half ride — brilliant BGM, cinematography and enough scares to disturb my sleep 😢😉
body:
I am basically a timid guy when it comes to horror movies. I got properly scared even while watching films like Chandramukhi and Arundhati 😢

So the only reason I voluntarily walked into VIRUPAKSHA was my unconditional love for good cinema — despite knowing exactly what I was doing to myself 😂

I wouldn’t categorise this as a pure horror film. For me, it is more of a THRILLER with supernatural elements.

And within that space, it delivers plenty of good thrills and twists, especially in the second half.

The BGM and cinematography are mind-blowing and constantly elevate the tempo and atmosphere of the movie.

The first half is slightly slow, particularly because of the love-story portions, but it uses that time to establish the characters and build a proper foundation.

Once the second half begins, the movie takes you on a very good thrill ride 👌

I personally felt Sai Dharam Tej was not the perfect fit for the character. His dialogue diction sounded a little numb to me and didn’t always match the confidence the character was supposed to project on screen.

But considering what he had gone through personally before this film, VIRUPAKSHA is still a very strong comeback for him 🙏

Samyuktha Menon is the show-stealer. She handles the crucial scenes almost effortlessly, and the rest of the cast also does its job very well.

There are naturally certain expectations when a filmmaker comes from Sukumar’s camp.

Director Karthik Varma Dandu meets those expectations for me and, at that point, was easily one of the strongest filmmakers to emerge from that school.

One creative choice I particularly loved is that the writer-director never feels the need to dismiss the supernatural elements as “myth” or suddenly force some pseudo-scientific explanation onto them.

The film simply respects the rules of its chosen genre and tells the story sincerely, irrespective of anyone’s personal beliefs 👌👌

PS: I am almost certain this movie is going to affect my sleep for the next few days 😢

All this suffering... just because of my unconditional love towards movies 😉

e: RAVANASURA shows the recurring problem when established heroes attempt darker roles but the film still feels obligated to protect the hero image. Ravi Teja as a baddie is the one interesting element; predictable justification, weak songs and average BGM prevent Sudheer Varma’s thriller from ever becoming exciting.
v: Ravi Teja’s psycho-negative shade is refreshing, but the movie is too scared to fully commit to its own darkness — eventually becoming neither offbeat nor satisfying commercial cinema 🤦‍♂️
body:
The major problem when established heroes try something genuinely new or offbeat is that many films refuse to dive completely into the genre.

Instead, they keep trying to balance the darker idea with familiar commercial-hero expectations — and eventually land in a space that is neither this nor that.

For me, RAVANASURA is a perfect example.

Whenever an established hero plays a negative or psychopathic character, Telugu commercial cinema seems to feel an unavoidable need for a later twist explaining that he is either pretending to be bad to catch the real criminals or killing only “bad people” because of some emotional flashback.

Basically... the hero image still needs to be protected 🤦‍♂️

The main reason I had hope for this film was director Sudheer Varma.

But man, he disappointed me to the core.

Ravi Teja playing a psychopathic, negative-shaded character is genuinely fresh and interesting to watch.

Unfortunately, at no point did I feel truly excited by that darkness because I was already expecting the screenplay to eventually explain why he is actually a “good person with a purpose.”

Ravi Teja’s negative shade is still the biggest positive of the movie.

Honestly, I felt he was far more interesting as a baddie than in the loud-comedy template that had become routine for him by then.

The songs are a BIG MINUS, and the BGM is only average.

Apart from Sudheer Varma’s name, the Ravanasura title song itself was one of the reasons I became curious about the film.

After watching it, I wasn’t even completely convinced that the title felt justified by the final characterisation 🤷🏻‍♂️

PS: I didn’t like Dhamaka either and that still became a hit 😜

So maybe Ravi Teja’s no-barriers-held negative characteristics here could still strike a chord with a section of movie lovers. For me, though, the film wastes the most interesting thing it had.

e: BALAGAM is the only movie in this archive that made me watch it twice before writing my experience. Its deeply rooted story proves that simple local lives can hold universal emotion, while Bheems’ music, natural performances and Venu Yeldandi’s surprisingly assured direction make the film feel lived rather than acted.
v: A rooted MASTERPIECE that made even this self-proclaimed RGV fan’s eyes wet 🙏 — simple Telangana life, beautiful emotions, lived-in performances and music straight from the heart.
body:
This is the only movie that made me watch it twice before writing about my experience.

And me — a self-proclaimed fan and follower of RGV — had my eyes wet with emotion in at least two or three scenes while watching this masterpiece 🙏🙏

Content-wise, BALAGAM once again proves something very important: if a writer stays connected to their roots, they are already surrounded by thousands of simple, beautiful and emotional stories waiting to be shared with the modern world.

You don’t always need a massive concept. Sometimes you just need to observe people honestly.

The songs, lyrics and BGM are the heart of this movie.

I was genuinely surprised to realise the music came from Bheems Ceciroleo, who I mostly associated at that time with out-and-out commercial cinema — his previous major album being Dhamaka 🙏

Almost every actor gives their best.

More importantly, I rarely felt as if they were “performing.” It often feels like you are simply watching these people live their characters and relationships 🙏🙏🙏

And finally, director Venu Yeldandi 👌👌

Who would have expected that a comedian — especially someone many people primarily knew from Jabardasth — could write and direct such deeply touching emotional content in his very first film?

He once again proves the old rule: don’t judge a book by its cover.

People like me who missed BALAGAM on the big screen should absolutely not miss it on OTT.

But honestly, after watching it... I wish I had experienced those emotions with a theatre full of people from the very beginning 🙏

e: Dasara had the ingredients for a stronger village political drama, but the writing shifts focus and never feels fully cooked. What keeps it engaging is Nani stepping convincingly into a raw mass role, supported by terrific cinematography, strong action staging and an effective BGM.
v: A half-cooked story rescued by Nani’s terrific raw performance, striking cinematography and some genuinely powerful action — ultimately a solid one-time watch.
body:
For me, Dasara is an average-to-good movie that is worth watching mainly for the performances of its lead cast and the raw cinematography.

Content-wise, the film had the potential to become a strong political drama set in a 1990s village.

But somewhere along the way, the writing seems eager to avoid obvious comparisons with Rangasthalam and shifts more of its focus towards the love-versus-lust angle.

Because of that, the core story feels a little half-cooked to me.

What the film lacks in writing depth, it tries to compensate for through some terrific visuals and raw action sequences.

The songs are only average for me, but the BGM works very well and lifts both the action and emotional scenes.

The biggest strength, without doubt, is Nani.

This is the first time I really saw him embrace such a raw, massy character. We can conveniently ignore a couple of earlier experiments in that zone 😜

Because audiences are so used to seeing Nani in boy-next-door roles, it takes a little time to sync with his rugged look and Telangana accent.

But once that adjustment happens, his performance is easily the most memorable part of the movie and once again proves what an excellent actor he is.

Overall, Dasara is a one-time watch for me — technically impressive and strongly performed, but with a story that could have gone much deeper.

e: Das Ki Dhamki works because Vishwak Sen commits completely to the commercial format while still giving himself room to perform. The first half is entertaining, the twists keep the screenplay moving, and his second role plus Leon James’ BGM give the film its strongest moments.
v: A proper commercial entertainer carried by Vishwak Sen — fun first half, well-placed twists, terrific second-character energy and a BGM that knows exactly when to kick in.
body:
I was never a big fan of Vishwak Sen initially, and I absolutely hated Falaknuma Das for its slow and overly realistic treatment 😅

But his performances in the films that followed gradually started grabbing my attention.

So I was genuinely curious to see how Das Ki Dhamki would turn out, especially because this was Vishwak attempting a full-length commercial entertainer in a much bigger way.

Content-wise, it is a proper commercial plot.

The first half is mostly focused on entertainment, songs and setting up the interval block.

Then comes the interval twist, followed by another major turn in the second half.

The structure itself is familiar, but Vishwak Sen’s direction and performance add considerable energy to it.

Acting-wise, he is at his casual best through most of the first half.

But it is the second character that really gives him room to show his acting range — and man, he simply nails it.

Some viewers may find portions of that performance a little overboard, but within this film’s commercial tone it worked for me.

Nivetha Pethuraj, on the other hand, felt slightly over-the-top in a few places, though that may also be because of the way her character was written.

The rest of the supporting cast does its job comfortably.

Special mention to Leon James’ BGM, which gives the action and suspense portions a very effective lift 🙏

Overall, Das Ki Dhamki is a good, entertaining watch and a film where Vishwak Sen’s confidence as both actor and filmmaker is clearly visible.

e: Ranga Maarthaanda may tell a broadly familiar story about ageing parents and changing family relationships, but the stage-artist perspective gives it added depth. Prakash Raj is predictably excellent, while Brahmanandam delivers the revelation of the film with a deeply emotional performance that completely changes how we see him.
v: A familiar family-drama theme transformed into a MUST WATCH by powerhouse performances — Prakash Raj is superb, but Brahmanandam revealing this emotional side is unforgettable 🙏
body:
A few years before Ranga Maarthaanda, I first came across the teaser of the Marathi film Natsamrat, starring the great Nana Patekar and directed by Mahesh Manjrekar.

It immediately grabbed my attention because both the actor and director were people I admired a lot.

I never managed to watch the original because of the language barrier, but I knew it had been critically acclaimed.

Years later, when I heard Krishna Vamsi was remaking the same story in Telugu with Prakash Raj, I became equally excited.

Another director and actor I admire were adapting a movie I had always wanted to experience — so this was one film I was determined to watch on the big screen irrespective of the talk 😊

At its core, the story travels through territory we have seen in films such as Baghban and several other family dramas: ageing parents, changing priorities, career-driven children and the emotional distance that can grow inside a family.

So the basic idea itself is not new.

What makes Ranga Maarthaanda more interesting is the way it integrates the life and identity of a stage artist into that familiar family conflict.

We already know how brilliant Prakash Raj can be, and this film simply reminds us why he is considered one of our finest actors.

But the real show-stealer for me is Brahmanandam.

Most of us grew up watching his comedy. His expressions became part of our everyday humour and, years later, our meme culture.

Here, the same man makes us cry.

His emotional performance is outstanding and reminds us that somewhere along the way we became so used to his comedy that we forgot what a complete actor he actually is 🙏🙏

I genuinely hope roles like this open another phase in his career.

Shivathmika is another pleasant surprise. Surrounded by such experienced performers, she still manages to make her presence felt.

Rahul Sipligunj and Anasuya also leave an impression in their respective roles.

Ilaiyaraaja’s music and BGM are soothing, the lyrics carry depth, and several dialogues have a strong philosophical quality.

What might otherwise have been merely a good watch built around a familiar theme becomes a MUST WATCH for me because of Brahmanandam and Prakash Raj.

e: Writer Padmabhushan moves through a pleasant but fairly average middle stretch before revealing the emotional idea that gives the film its identity. The final thirty minutes are the heart of the movie, with Rohini and Ashish Vidyarthi emerging as the true show-stealers alongside an effortless Suhas.
v: A modest film that saves its best for the final 30 minutes — once the real emotion lands, Rohini and Ashish Vidyarthi turn a simple story into a genuine MUST WATCH ❤️
body:
I still can’t believe I missed Writer Padmabhushan on the big screen 😞

For its core emotion alone, this is a MUST WATCH.

The movie starts on a good note, then moves through a fairly average stretch with bits of entertainment here and there.

And then the final thirty minutes arrive.

That section is the heart of the film and completely changes the overall experience.

Without that emotional payoff, Writer Padmabhushan might have remained an average feel-good movie for me.

With it, the story suddenly finds a much deeper purpose.

Suhas makes the lead role look effortless — by this point, this kind of natural performance almost feels like a cakewalk for him.

But the real show-stealers are Rohini and Ashish Vidyarthi 🙏🙏🙏

Their performances give the final portions the emotional weight the story needs.

I do feel the film could have been mounted and crafted even better, because the central emotion deserved the strongest possible presentation.

Budget limitations may have led to some compromises.

Still, the scenes and screenplay retain a natural quality, and when the film finally reveals what it really wants to say, the emotion lands beautifully.

That final stretch is what stayed with me — and it is the reason Writer Padmabhushan rises well above its otherwise simple packaging.

e: Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar follows Luv Ranjan’s familiar relationship-comedy template, but Ranbir Kapoor and Shraddha Kapoor bring fresh chemistry and the film finds its strongest rhythm after the interval. The crazy climax is exactly the kind of comic escape that makes the whole conflict work without over-explaining it.
v: Classic Luv Ranjan territory with a fresher pair and even more entertainment — the first half takes time, but the interval, second half and gloriously mad climax make it a very good watch.
body:
If you enjoy Luv Ranjan’s style of films, Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar is another easy recommendation.

It follows the familiar Luv Ranjan template — fast dialogue, relationship confusion, exaggerated emotional logic and comedy built around modern romance.

So yes, bits and pieces may remind you of his earlier movies.

But for me, this one has much more entertainment value 👌

The first half does the necessary setup, although I felt it could have been tighter and funnier.

The real strengths are the interval block, the second half and that absolutely crazy climax.

Ranbir Kapoor and Shraddha Kapoor make a fresh onscreen pair and their chemistry works very well. Both are completely comfortable with the film’s energetic dialogue-heavy tone.

The die-hard Luv Ranjan fan in me still missed the old combination of Kartik Aaryan and Nushrratt Bharuccha, because I kept imagining how naturally they might have fitted into this world 😄

So their guest appearances were a very pleasant surprise.

The supporting cast is uniformly good, and Dimple Kapadia once again gets a memorable part and has great fun with it.

My favourite decision is the climax.

I kept wondering how the director would resolve the central conflict without making one side look completely wrong.

Instead of getting trapped in heavy justification, he simply chooses madness — and turns the finale into a laugh riot 🤣

By that point you are enjoying the chaos too much to demand a courtroom-style explanation.

Overall, Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar is a very good watch — especially if Luv Ranjan’s brand of relationship comedy already works for you.

e: Pathaan worked for me as exactly the comeback vehicle Shah Rukh Khan needed: unapologetically large, stylish and crowd-pleasing. The film may not be technically flawless, but its cast, action, terrific BGM and Spy Universe ambition make those imperfections very easy to ignore.
v: SRK’s comeback is a full-blown big-screen celebration — swagger, action, BGM, glamour, twists and Salman-sized madness packed into one wildly entertaining spy spectacle.
body:
EXCELLENT TREAT!!!!! 😍

I walked out of Pathaan still completely charged by the experience, and this is absolutely the kind of film I could watch multiple times.

Hindi cinema had been going through a difficult theatrical phase, with several big films failing to connect and dubbed releases taking an increasingly large share of the box office.

And then, after four years away from a full-fledged starring vehicle, Shah Rukh Khan returned with exactly the kind of larger-than-life movie his fans were waiting for.

And of course, Bhai Jaan turns up to add his own helping hand to the madness 🙏🤣

Pathaan has enough story and emotion to support its spectacle, while the cast throws itself fully into the action.

SRK has the swagger, Deepika Padukone is terrific in both the action and glamour portions, and John Abraham gets the presence needed for a proper big-screen antagonist.

Technically, the film is not perfect.

But the pace, scale and entertainment are strong enough that I simply did not care about every imperfection while watching it.

The BGM is terrific, the production values are suitably huge, and the action keeps trying to go bigger.

Most importantly, this feels like a perfect comeback film for SRK.

A neutral audience can enjoy the spectacle; a die-hard Shah Rukh fan will probably spend half the runtime screaming 😍

I also liked how Pathaan expands the YRF Spy Universe. In the same way a major crossover film can suddenly make separate characters feel part of one larger world, this movie makes the future possibilities of the franchise much more exciting.

To put the experience in one very simple filmi checklist:

Content? Irukuuu!!!
Character arcs? Irukuuu!!!
Emotion? Irukuuu!!!
Twists? Irukuuu!!!
Grand visuals? Irukuuu!!!
Action? Irukuuu!!!
BGM? Irukuuu!!!
Songs? Irukuuu!!!
Hotness? Irukuuu!!!

And when you want complete physics-defying BANG BANG?

Salman Khan Irukuuu!!! 🤣🔥

For me, Pathaan is pure big-screen entertainment and one of those star vehicles that understands exactly what its audience came to celebrate.

e: Waltair Veerayya is formula cinema with limited story impact, but Bobby understands the nostalgic Chiranjeevi flavour his audience wants. The Srikakulam dialect, comedy timing and dance staging bring flashes of vintage Chiru even though the Ravi Teja track and climax never deliver the expected high.
v: Poonakalu raaledhu… kaani time-pass ayipoyindi 😄 Routine story, ordinary music and a weak final stretch, but vintage Chiru comedy, dialect and dances make it a decent one-time watch.
body:
Poonakalu raaledhu… kaani time-pass ayipoyindi 😄

Bobby, a self-proclaimed Chiranjeevi fan, clearly wanted to present Chiru in the massy, comic avatar that helped make him the Mega Star.

On that front, Waltair Veerayya gives fans plenty of nostalgic moments.

The main drawbacks are the lack of truly impactful content and the fact that Chiru’s look in a few portions does not carry the same effortless grace we remember from his peak years.

The story itself is ordinary and the screenplay follows a very familiar commercial formula.

But it has been a long time since Chiranjeevi played this kind of character, and that alone makes the film reasonably entertaining for a normal viewer while giving long-time fans a stronger vintage kick.

I personally got flashes of Annayya, Shankar Dada and Andarivaadu from the massy presentation, Srikakulam dialect and especially the comedy timing.

And that proves something important: whatever changes age may bring visually, Chiru’s comic timing is still very much intact.

If a director gives him a genuinely funny out-and-out entertainer, I still believe he can do wonders 🙏

The little Jambalakadi Jaaru Mitaya bit is a perfect example of that old-school ease 👌

The songs and BGM are pretty ordinary for me and do not add much impact.

The dances, however, are deliberately choreographed to bring back that vintage Chiru feeling, and those portions work.

The bigger disappointment comes in the second half.

The heavily hyped combination with Ravi Teja never gives me the expected Poonakalu. I wanted much more from that track than a fairly routine backstory.

The pre-climax and climax also try to do something different, but those ideas never gel properly with the rest of the film.

Overall, Waltair Veerayya is a one-time watch with routine direction and not-so-great content.

But as a Chiranjeevi film after his comeback, it is still a considerably better and more enjoyable outing than several of the films around it.

e: Veera Simha Reddy is designed almost entirely as Balakrishna fan-service. Gopichand Malineni lands a few elevations and political punches, but the familiar dual-role structure, repetitive fights and underwhelming music leave the film without the content needed to make those highs memorable.
v: Plenty of Balayya elevation, but very little fresh content beneath it — hardcore fans may enjoy the punches, yet the recycled dual-role template and repetitive action make this far less impactful than Akhanda, Simha or Legend.
body:
Veera Simha Reddy once again reminded me of one thing: when it comes to combining huge Balakrishna elevations with genuinely strong mass content, Boyapati still understands that formula better than most.

Gopichand Malineni is himself a Balayya fan, and that affection is visible everywhere.

There are good elevation shots and a few political punches that will definitely excite the hardcore fan base.

But the film does not have enough fresh content underneath those moments.

The story follows an extremely familiar Balakrishna template: dual roles, the younger character largely existing in the shadow of the much more powerful senior character, and an elaborate backstory explaining the senior character’s conflict.

The sister sentiment tries to add an emotional layer, but even that reminded me of territory we have travelled through in earlier faction dramas.

Apart from the oora-mass fight in Istanbul, very little in the action felt new to me.

The movie has fight after fight, yet most of them use almost the same grammar — change the fighters, change the background, repeat the elevation 🙏

Thaman’s music and BGM were a massive asset in films such as Akhanda.

Here, they never gel with the material strongly enough to create the same impact.

The director’s intention is very clear: this movie is made primarily to serve the hardcore Balayya audience.

The funniest proof is probably having a major praise song called “Jai Balayya” when nobody inside the story is actually named Balayya or Balakrishna 🤣

Akhanda and Unstoppable had helped Balakrishna connect again with a wider set of younger and family audiences.

That is why I felt disappointed to see him return to such a familiar, narrowly fan-oriented subject.

The movie may still work commercially because of its mass format and festival timing.

But for me, it does not leave anything close to the impact created by Simha, Legend or Akhanda.

e: Dhamaka doubles down on Trinadha Rao Nakkina’s familiar mix of loud comedy, convenient logic and manufactured sentiment. That formula may still work for its target mass audience, but for me it became so tiring that I walked out before the climax — while once again missing the effortless comic Ravi Teja of Venky and Dubai Seenu.
v: The last Ravi Teja film that made me leave before the climax was Khatarnak… and Dhamaka somehow joined that club 🙏 Loud, illogical and exhausting — mass formula without the Ravi Teja comedy I actually miss.
body:
When was the last time I walked out of a movie without even waiting for the climax?

Khatarnak.

And bingo… Ravi Teja managed to bring me back to that feeling with Dhamaka 🙏

When Trinadha Rao Nakkina directs a film, you generally know the flavour you are going to get.

Like Cinema Choopistha Mava and Nenu Local, Dhamaka is packed with an illogical plot, convenient characters, loud over-the-top comedy and forced sentiment presented in the name of middle-class emotion.

Somehow, that exact formula has worked commercially for him before.

And Dhamaka is basically that template turned up to maximum volume.

My bigger disappointment is with Ravi Teja.

I am not sure why the Mass Maharaja has increasingly been chasing supposedly powerful hero characters instead of leaning into the loose, effortless mass-entertainer space that once suited him so naturally.

I genuinely miss the Ravi Teja comedy of Venky and Dubai Seenu 😞

Trinadha Rao at least stays completely committed to his target audience.

He is clearly not bothered about whether the so-called multiplex crowd approves of the logic, tone or excess.

He knows the B- and C-centre mass audience he wants to entertain and makes the movie for them without apology.

So I would not be shocked if the film works very well with that crowd.

But for me, Dhamaka was such a tiring experience that I did not even feel the need to stay until the end.

e: Cirkus contains all the ingredients of Rohit Shetty’s established comedy school — exaggerated characters, broad reactions and unapologetically loud humour. I normally have no problem enjoying that style, but this time the laughs are too sparse and even the better gags feel recycled from his own earlier films.
v: A one-time watch at best. I usually enjoy Rohit Shetty’s proudly over-the-top comedy, but Cirkus repeats the same faces and comic beats with far too few actual laughs.
body:
One-time watch… at best.

Cirkus is a typical Rohit Shetty comedy filled with deliberately over-the-top performances, forced chaos and exaggerated characters.

Kids and a section of the audience may enjoy that style completely, while others may find it unbearable.

But that has always been the nature of Rohit Shetty’s comedy.

Personally, I enjoy very different genres and I respect the fact that every filmmaker has a particular style.

I try to cache-clear my mind before every film 😄 and judge it within the kind of movie it is trying to be, rather than demanding the same sensibility from everyone.

That is exactly why I have happily enjoyed Rohit Shetty’s outrageous comedy in films such as All the Best, the Golmaal series and Bol Bachchan.

His humour is loud, but it is generally not dependent on vulgarity or double meaning — and when the timing works, the madness can be genuinely funny.

Unfortunately, Cirkus just did not work for me.

There were very few proper laughs.

Even the comedy portions that did land kept giving me the feeling that I had already seen the same joke, reaction or character dynamic somewhere before — and quite possibly in another Rohit Shetty movie itself.

Repeating the same group of comic actors in similar types of roles probably adds to that déjà vu.

Ranveer Singh is effortless with the exaggerated tone the film asks from him.

Jacqueline, unfortunately, has almost nothing useful to do 😉

I went in fully prepared for Rohit Shetty-style nonsense.

The problem was not the nonsense — it was that this time, the nonsense simply was not funny enough.

e: Avatar: The Way of Water is extraordinary filmmaking craft, particularly once James Cameron takes us underwater, but my reaction was more mixed than expected. The long first-hour setup reduced the excitement and, having lived through the original Avatar phenomenon, I never recovered that same sense of discovery despite appreciating the technology behind it.
v: A technical masterpiece that I admired more than I was awestruck by. The water world is beautiful, but the slow setup and impossible expectations kept it from recreating the original Avatar’s once-in-a-generation WOW factor.
body:
I came out of Avatar: The Way of Water with mixed feelings.

To be completely frank, the AWE and WOW factor I experienced with the first Avatar was missing this time.

The original film took us by surprise.

James Cameron’s scale of visualisation — and the enormous technical effort behind creating that world — felt revolutionary on screen.

More than a decade later, the problem for the sequel is partly its own legacy.

The expectations are gigantic.

And the first hour moves so slowly towards the core of the new story that portions almost felt like unseen scenes from the original Avatar being restored years later.

By the time the film finally moves properly into the water world, some of my initial enthusiasm had already dropped 😞

That said, the introduction to this new environment is beautifully designed and communicated.

The underwater sequences are technically excellent.

But even there, I did not experience the same shock of discovery that the first movie gave me.

The experience becomes more impressive when you understand the challenge Cameron and his team took on — developing and adapting performance-capture technology to work convincingly underwater.

That is where I can absolutely admire the film as a technical masterpiece.

But that is also the complication.

Most audiences are not going to sit in a theatre thinking about what new technology had to be invented or how difficult a shot was to achieve.

They will simply ask whether the movie is engaging and whether the CGI still creates magic.

Bottom line: if you have never experienced Avatar before, The Way of Water is absolutely worth seeing on the biggest screen possible — especially with kids.

But if you lived through the hysteria and technical shock of the first Avatar, keep your expectations under control.

The craft remains extraordinary; the feeling of discovering Pandora for the first time is much harder to recreate.

e: Love Today takes one of the most ordinary anxieties of modern relationships — handing your unlocked phone to someone else — and turns it into sharp, hugely entertaining cinema with a meaningful message. Pradeep Ranganathan’s writing, direction and lead performance make the concept feel both funny and uncomfortably familiar.
v: MAN!!! A wonderfully relevant idea for the smartphone generation — hilarious, uncomfortable and meaningful at the same time. A genuine MUST WATCH for anyone who guards their phone like a national secret 😄
body:
Finally got the chance to watch Love Today on the big screen and… MAN!!!

This is such a relevant idea for the world we live in, with a beautiful message delivered through genuinely entertaining cinema.

Honestly, it does not matter where or how you watch this movie.

For me, it is a MUST WATCH for practically everyone living with a smartphone today.

Our phones have become such an integral part of our lives that many of us feel uncomfortable handing them to another person even for a few seconds 😄

That tiny modern anxiety becomes the foundation for the entire film.

And because the situation is so familiar, the comedy and relationship conflicts connect immediately.

The movie does not merely use phones as a gimmick.

It explores trust, privacy, insecurity and the versions of ourselves that exist inside our digital lives — while making sure the message never kills the entertainment.

Every actor and technician does justice to the script.

And while looking up the technical team after watching the movie, I was genuinely surprised to realise that Pradeep Ranganathan — the lead actor — also wrote and directed the film 🙏🙏🙏

That makes the achievement even more impressive.

Love Today takes a very current behavioural truth, turns it into a laugh riot, and still leaves you with something meaningful to think about after the laughs stop.

e: Yashoda tackles a sensitive subject through disturbing imagery and an increasingly uneasy thriller setup. The interval and post-interval portions are deliberately uncomfortable, while Samantha leads a strong cast and Mani Sharma’s BGM keeps a constant sense that something is wrong beneath the surface.
v: A hard-hitting thriller that genuinely made us uncomfortable — not for the sensitive-hearted, but Samantha, the unsettling premise and Mani Sharma’s BGM make it a compelling MUST WATCH for those who can handle the subject.
body:
I came out of Yashoda not quite sure how to describe the experience.

The story and some of the visuals are definitely not for the sensitive-hearted 🙏

Especially around the interval and immediately after it, the film deliberately makes you uncomfortable.

Even after leaving the theatre, my wife and I were still debating whether the shivers were because of the multiplex AC on a winter night or because of what we had just watched 😄

Meanwhile, my daughter seemed far less disturbed and was watching with complete curiosity — even asking us questions about surrogacy!

That probably says a lot about how differently this subject can affect different viewers.

If you are comfortable watching hard-hitting films that include a few unpleasant visuals, then for me Yashoda is a must watch.

It takes on a very sensitive subject and builds a thriller around it without softening the discomfort too much.

Samantha is at her usual best, both in the performance and action portions.

Unni Mukundan and Varalaxmi Sarathkumar get substantial roles and make good use of them.

Rao Ramesh and Murali Sharma handle their portions effortlessly, even though the characters do not demand anything radically different from them.

Mani Sharma’s BGM is another major strength.

Throughout the first half, it keeps creating that constant feeling that something is fishy underneath the polished surface — and that mood helps the thriller enormously.

Writer-director duo Hari and Harish do a good job with both the premise and execution.

The CG work could certainly have been much better, but it did not take away the impact of the central idea for me.

Overall, Yashoda is an unsettling but engaging thriller that works precisely because it is willing to make its audience uncomfortable.

e: Kantara begins with a familiar landlord-versus-tribal conflict but becomes something far more immersive through folklore, raw staging, spectacular sound and Rishab Shetty’s complete creative commitment. The final twenty minutes are the kind of cinematic madness that make the theatre itself feel like part of the experience.
v: Just VAAAAAVVVV!!! A simple conflict transformed into a raw audiovisual JAATHAARAAA — terrific visuals, BGM, performances and action, with Rishab Shetty’s astonishing final stretch turning it into a big-screen MASTERPIECE.
body:
Just VAAAAAVVVV!!!!!!

At its core, Kantara begins with a fairly old and familiar conflict — landlord versus tribal community.

But the way Rishab Shetty blends that simple foundation with local folklore, raw visuals, terrific BGM, powerful performances and superbly staged action is what turns the film into a MASTERPIECE for me.

Your eyes and ears simply cannot wander away from what is being served on the big screen.

If there is one film from the recent past that I would say should absolutely not be missed in a theatre, this is THE ONE.

Rishab Shetty — take a bow, man! 🙏

Before watching the film, I had obviously seen all the praise about him being the writer, director and lead actor.

After watching it, I actually felt he may have had no other option but to wear all three hats.

The idea on paper is so rooted in a specific culture, mood and instinct that it would probably be difficult for another person to completely understand what he imagined and then translate it to the screen with the same conviction.

And what he does onscreen in the final twenty minutes is something else entirely.

TERRIFIC!!!

The whole movie is handled in an unapologetically raw and rustic manner.

The characters feel part of that world rather than performers who have been placed inside a carefully decorated set.

The sound, camera work, physicality and folklore keep building on one another until the final stretch explodes.

All that said, Kantara may not be for every regular moviegoer.

If your only expectation is easy entertainment, or if you need conventional storytelling to guide every beat, the film’s rhythm and rootedness may not work for you.

But if you want a different visual and audio experience on the big screen… you are in for a full-on JAATHAARAAA!!!!! 🔥

It is also wonderful to see Kannada cinema finding such a powerful national voice in recent years.

Special credit to filmmakers and banners such as Hombale Films for backing stories that are deeply local yet cinematic enough to travel far beyond their original market 🙏🙏🙏

e: The Ghost has several technically strong ingredients — Praveen Sattaru’s direction, an interesting screenplay structure, well-edited fights and an effective BGM. Unfortunately, the routine and underwritten core story never creates enough involvement, leaving all that craft functioning mainly as a saving grace.
v: Good direction, sharp action and a damn-good BGM trying desperately to rescue a below-average story. Stylish on the surface, but the content never hooks you enough for The Ghost to become more than average.
body:
Average!!!

The frustrating thing about The Ghost is that there is actually a lot of good work on screen.

The direction is good, the screenplay has interesting moments, the BGM is strong, and the fights are very well choreographed and edited.

But almost all of that effort is weakened by a below-average core story.

The content never really pulls you into what is happening.

Instead of becoming strengths that elevate a good story, the technical departments end up functioning mainly as saving graces for material that never becomes involving enough.

Even the title — The Ghost — sounds much more powerful and mysterious than the story ultimately feels.

That mismatch also raises expectations that the actual film struggles to satisfy.

I expected much more from Praveen Sattaru.

His direction itself is not the problem; he stages the action and atmosphere well.

But this time the routine action-film foundation simply does not give him enough to work with.

The BGM is damn good and gives the action portions the lift they need.

Nagarjuna, despite age naturally catching up, puts in the effort required to fit the action-heavy role.

There is not a great deal of dramatic range demanded from the character, so the performance is mostly about presence and physical attitude.

Ultimately, The Ghost is a stylishly assembled action film built around content that is far too ordinary.

Good craft can disguise that weakness for a while — but it cannot completely save it.

e: GodFather worked for me as a strong Chiranjeevi comeback vehicle despite abandoning many of his usual commercial ingredients. The political-thriller setup lets his screen presence and expressions dominate, while Satyadev makes brilliant use of his biggest mainstream platform and repeatedly stands toe-to-toe with the film’s stars.
v: After Sye Raa and Acharya… finally MEGA BOSS IS BACK! Chiru’s eyes do the mass work, Satyadev nearly steals the film, and Salman happily murders physics so everyone else can stay respectable 😜
body:
After an average Sye Raa and the debacle of Acharya… finally, MEGA BOSS IS BACK!!!

There was surprisingly little buzz around GodFather before release.

It was a remake whose Malayalam original, Lucifer, was already easily accessible to Telugu audiences, and Acharya had obviously damaged expectations as well.

But I was still eager to watch it because Chiranjeevi has historically had a terrific record with remakes — not just commercially, but often in adapting them into something that fits his own screen personality.

I had not watched Lucifer before seeing GodFather, so I went in without trying to compare every scene or performance with the original.

And on its own terms, I found the film to be a full meal for Mega fans.

Interestingly, it does this without relying heavily on many of the standard Chiranjeevi ingredients.

There is no constant comedy track, no regular lineup of trademark songs, and very little opportunity for those charming dance moves.

Yet Chiru’s GodFather still manages to enthral.

His expressive eyes have always been one of his biggest assets, and a controlled political thriller gives him plenty of opportunity to use them instead of constantly chasing louder mass moments 🙏

But the biggest acting surprise for me is Satyadev.

He has always been an asset to Telugu cinema, and this felt like his first truly huge platform to showcase that talent to a broad mass audience.

He uses the opportunity completely.

Standing opposite performers such as Chiranjeevi, Nayanthara, Murali Sharma and Salman Khan is not easy, yet in a few scenes Satyadev actually walks away with the limelight.

That is genuinely commendable 🙏🙏🙏

Nayanthara, Murali Sharma and the rest of the cast fit their roles comfortably.

The writing and direction team also does a good job adapting the material.

Even knowing that it was a remake, I never felt as though I was simply watching somebody mechanically reproduce another film.

Thaman’s BGM gives Chiru some solid elevation — particularly those Mega-eye moments 😄 — although after hearing what he delivered in Akhanda, I still felt he could have gone even harder here.

And then there is Salman Bhai.

These days every over-the-top commercial fight gets trolled for violating physics… unless it belongs to a film stylish enough to convince people not to care.

GodFather finds a genius solution: simply bring Salman into those portions so all physics-related trolling can be redirected towards him 😉🤣

Salman does exactly what Salman knows best.

Physics ki KCPD chesi vadiladu!!!

I still demand a full Boyapati–Salman Khan collaboration someday.

Iddaru kalisi physics ni Bang Bang Bang chesestharu 🥸

Overall, GodFather gave me what I wanted most at that point — a confident Chiranjeevi film that reminded me how much screen presence he still has when the material stops fighting against his strengths.

e: Lovers’ Love Stori takes a risky non-linear approach, beginning close to the pre-climax and then gradually revealing its characters’ backstories. Directors Vempati Srenivas and Venugopal Makala make that structure work surprisingly well, with Dhruvan Katakam providing the strongest emotional connection despite the film’s obvious production limitations.
v: A small indie film with genuinely good content and a clever screenplay — the cast has limitations, but the writing keeps you glued and the passion behind the camera is visible in every department.
body:
Good content and good screenplay!!!

Lovers’ Love Stori takes a storytelling route that is not particularly easy to pull off.

Instead of beginning traditionally, it starts close to the pre-climax and then gradually reveals the backstories of its characters.

That kind of structure can be risky in a non-thriller.

If the audience already starts predicting the ending, there is always a chance they will lose interest in what is currently happening on screen and spend the rest of the runtime simply waiting to see whether their guess is correct.

But directors Vempati Srenivas and Venugopal Makala manage the screenplay well enough to keep the focus on the present proceedings.

The fact that the same duo produced, directed and contributed to the dialogues also makes their passion for the project very visible.

Among the performances, Dhruvan Katakam stands out.

His character is the one I connected with most immediately, and he does a fantastic job carrying that emotional connection.

The rest of the cast is okay within their limitations.

With a few more experienced or recognisable performers from the short-film space, I feel the same content could have been elevated another level.

The BGM and song lyrics stay in line with the story and never try to overpower a film that clearly knows its production scale.

That applies to most departments — everybody seems to understand what the movie needs rather than trying to show off beyond the material.

For an independently produced Telugu film, Lovers’ Love Stori is a very sincere effort with a screenplay that deserves appreciation.

e: Oke Oka Jeevitham has a beautiful emotional idea about regret, missed choices and the temptation to revisit the past, but the execution never feels as strong as the writing deserves. The first half is slow and the music adds little, while Vennela Kishore, Priyadarshi and the nostalgic details help the second half become the real soul of the film.
v: GOOD content, uneven execution. The first half drags and some emotional beats lose power, but nostalgia, Vennela Kishore’s painfully relatable track and a much stronger second half save the journey.
body:
GOOD content, but weak execution!!!

Oke Oka Jeevitham is built around an idea that can connect very strongly with people who carry regret about their past — whether that regret comes from career choices, studies, relationships or simply wishing they had been more confident at a particular point in life.

For viewers who do not personally connect with that feeling, the story may land as only an okay time-travel drama.

My issue is not really with the central idea.

The writing has plenty of emotional potential.

But somewhere in the execution, the film never extracts everything that is present on paper.

It is difficult to point to one single technical problem, yet the overall experience repeatedly feels like it could have been handled much better.

The songs and BGM are only okay for me and, rather than strengthening the emotion, occasionally feel like a minus.

The much-discussed casting of Amala Akkineni also did not work as strongly for me as I expected.

Her introductory shot is a sweet little tribute to her real-life work with Blue Cross and clearly shows how much the director wanted her in the film.

But in the mother-son portions, I felt the limitations in her performance reduced some of the emotional impact of scenes that were otherwise very well written.

Sharwanand is the nominal hero, but Priyadarshi and Vennela Kishore are equally important to the film’s emotional structure.

For me, Kishore’s character is probably the most instantly relatable.

His regrets send many of us straight back into a guilt trip about our own study and career choices 😢

Priyadarshi’s track, meanwhile, takes us back to all those innocent school-crush memories 😍

The first half contains several small nostalgic details, but the overall pace feels slow and slightly laggy while it sets up the premise.

The second half is the soul and saving grace of the film.

That is where the central idea finally starts delivering the emotion I expected from the beginning.

Oke Oka Jeevitham is therefore a movie I liked more for what it wanted to say than for how consistently it said it.

e: Brahmāstra worked for me very differently from many of the reviews I read after the show. I enjoyed the mythology-inspired content, Ayan Mukerji’s ambition and the cast, while the VFX — widely praised elsewhere — was actually the element I found least convincing. It is a divisive film, but one I was happy to watch again.
v: I know this was not the popular reaction, but I genuinely loved it 😄 Good content, ambitious visualisation, a huge cast and franchise potential — the irony is that the graphics were actually my biggest complaint.
body:
Personally, I loved Brahmāstra.

For me, it had good content, ambitious visualisation from the director’s perspective, a great star cast and strong performances.

Ironically, the one department that disappointed me most was the graphics.

With more consistently convincing visual effects, I think this could have been a genuinely great theatrical watch.

There is one concept I still could not completely understand though — why exactly does the hero’s fire become especially active whenever the heroine is around?

Vaadu em fire gurinchi maatladuthunnado 😉

I watched an early show, and only after coming out did I start reading the flood of reviews.

That was when I became genuinely surprised.

A large number of reactions seemed almost completely opposite to my own experience.

Many people were praising the graphics while criticising the content.

I had felt almost exactly the reverse 🤷🏻‍♂️

For a moment I actually wondered whether I had watched the movie differently from everyone else.

I mentally replayed the experience, even cross-checked with the friend who watched it with me, and still came back to the same conclusion.

For the kind of fantasy story Brahmāstra chooses to tell, I found the content interesting and felt there was real potential to build a larger franchise around this universe.

That does not mean everyone has to experience it the same way.

This is clearly one of those films that connects very differently with different audiences.

My suggestion is simple: watch it and form your own opinion.

I was happy enough with the experience that I was already planning a second watch with my daughter.

I also think kids are likely to enjoy the fantasy-adventure side of it much more freely than adults who are analysing every dialogue and effect.

And before anyone suspects a paid positive review — no one in the film industry even knows I exist, so bribing me would be a very inefficient marketing strategy 🤣

This was simply my genuine experience, and yours may be completely different based on your taste.

e: Liger is frustrating because Puri Jagannadh’s films have often survived weak plots through explosive characterisation and sharp dialogue. Here, the Pan-India ambition strips away exactly those strengths, leaving an old-school masala structure without the attitude that once made his formula entertaining.
v: DISASTER!!!! Puri went Pan-India and somehow left his own biggest strengths behind — no kickass characterisation, no trademark dialogue fire, stale masala everywhere, and Ramya Krishna almost alone in trying to save it.
body:
DISASTER!!!!

Puri and Vijay Deverakonda went Pan-India… and somewhere along the journey the movie seems to have forgotten what makes a Puri Jagannadh film work in the first place 😭

Puri has never really depended on complex stories.

His biggest strength has always been the kickass characterisation and those hard-hitting dialogues that give even familiar plots a unique attitude.

That dialogue energy is often the actual kick his audience comes for.

And much to my disappointment, that is exactly what is missing in Liger.

You go into a Puri film expecting the hero to explode with outrageous confidence and high-octane lines.

But here the central character’s stammer is written so prominently that there is barely room for even ordinary dialogue delivery, forget the classic Puri-style verbal punches 😞

In the quest to make a giant Pan-India film, Puri seems to have abandoned the one strength that has repeatedly rescued his weaker stories over the years.

Ananya Panday was at her annoying best for me.

Ramya Krishna is basically the only real saving grace.

I went into Liger with genuine curiosity because I have always been a huge fan of Puri Jagannadh’s hard-hitting dialogue style.

Also, the audience had clearly begun changing.

Films with strong content were finding huge success while routine masala movies were increasingly being rejected.

Even up to iSmart Shankar, Puri was still working inside a familiar old formula.

So with Liger being mounted on such a huge Pan-India scale, I was genuinely curious to see whether he would reinvent himself.

Instead, he somehow makes things worse by sticking to the same stale masala structure minus the trademark Puri dialogue and character style that made that formula enjoyable in the first place.

That is what makes Liger more disappointing than merely bad.

e: Karthikeya 2 expands the original beautifully into a larger treasure-hunt adventure without losing the intellectual curiosity that made the first film interesting. Chandoo Mondeti keeps faith and scepticism in conversation with each other, then surrounds that idea with strong locations, cinematography, BGM and purposeful characters.
v: EXCELLENT, BRILLIANT and a PERFECT SEQUEL!!! A gripping treasure hunt that lets faith and rationality challenge each other instead of choosing an easy side — backed by terrific visuals, BGM and a filmmaker in complete control.
body:
EXCELLENT, BRILLIANT and a PERFECT SEQUEL!!!!

Karthikeya made me a fan of Chandoo Mondeti with his very first film.

A few of the movies that followed did not work as well for me, but with Karthikeya 2 he comes roaring back.

If you watch the film simply as a movie instead of entering the theatre determined to take either the theist or atheist side, there is a lot to enjoy here.

At heart, this is a treasure-hunt adventure with a good dose of thrills, mythology, belief, scepticism and curiosity.

What impressed me is that the writing does not allow only one side to dominate all the time.

In some scenes faith gets the upper hand; in others rational questioning becomes more important.

Both are used to keep the story moving rather than to turn the movie into a lecture.

That balance itself shows the intelligence of the writer-director 🙏

Some of the film’s ideas stayed with me long after the show — especially the thought that understanding what we believe is more important than blindly worshipping it, and that blindly accepting science can be just as limiting as blindly accepting faith.

The larger message for me is simple: do not believe anything blindly, but do not reject everything blindly either.

Once such a gripping idea is supported by terrific cinematography, strong locations and a superb BGM, the movie becomes both a visual and audio treat.

I also liked that practically every major character has a purpose in the story rather than appearing only to fill screen time.

The cast does a very good job carrying those different shades of belief, doubt and adventure.

I am a huge fan of the first Karthikeya, and Part 2 did not disappoint me even for a second.

Now I am simply waiting for the third chapter of this franchise 🔥

e: Bimbisara starts with a fresh reversal of the usual time-travel setup — sending a man from the past into the present — but rushes through too much of its promising first half. The second half works better and Kalyan Ram carries almost the entire film, making it an above-average watch rather than the knockout the concept could have delivered.
v: A genuinely exciting time-travel idea that deserved a better first half. Kalyan Ram gives it everything and the second half saves the film, but the blockbuster talk felt bigger than the movie I actually watched.
body:
I came out of Bimbisara feeling one thing very strongly: it was overrated.

I usually try to ignore the talk around a film and get involved with whatever is actually happening on screen.

But this time, the gap between the blockbuster reactions I had heard and my own experience was impossible to ignore.

On paper, the basic concept is excellent.

Most time-travel movies I had seen were built around someone from the present or future travelling into the past.

Here, the more interesting twist is having a man from the distant past suddenly thrown into the modern world.

Aditya 369 touched parts of that idea, but it is still not something our mainstream cinema explores very often.

With such a strong concept in hand, I felt the film should have been much better.

The first half is in too much of a hurry and does not allow the premise to breathe.

The second half is what saves the movie and finally begins using the setup more effectively.

Considering this was Mallidi Vassishta’s directorial debut, though, the ambition itself deserves appreciation.

The film gives very little space for anyone except Kalyan Ram.

He puts in enormous effort and practically carries the movie on his shoulders.

I still did not feel he could completely justify every shade the role demanded, but it is unquestionably a committed performance and a very good effort from him.

Keeravani’s BGM is effective in places, although several portions reminded me strongly of the sound worlds of Baahubali and RRR.

My feeling is that Bimbisara benefited from a smart combination of controlled budget, good release timing, proper publicity and an audience that was hungry for stronger Telugu content at that point.

Those factors helped turn it into a major commercial success.

Judged only by what I watched on screen, though, I would place it as an above-average movie built around an excellent idea that could have been executed far better.

e: Sita Ramam overcame probably the biggest obstacle possible for a romance: me 😄 I went in reluctantly, expecting another love story, and was completely absorbed from the opening titles. Hanu Raghavapudi’s world, Dulquer and Mrunal’s chemistry, the writing, music and visual craft combine into one of those rare romantic films I was genuinely glad not to miss on the big screen.
v: I hate love stories… and still walked out calling this a CLASSIC ❤️ Great content, casting, acting, dialogues, music, locations, direction and production all falling beautifully into place.
body:
Before anything else, one confession: I generally hate love stories 😄

Some of the romantic movies other people call classics have literally put me to sleep in theatres, and more than once I have gone only because my wife wanted to watch them.

The last romantic film I remember genuinely loving was Malli Malli Idi Rani Roju — and I still regret not watching that one on the big screen.

So I am very glad I did not make the same mistake with Sita Ramam.

I had already heard all the rave reviews, but I was still reluctant because in my mind it was simply “another love story.”

My wife finally forced the issue — partly because of her own love for Dulquer Salmaan 😄 — and I am glad I surrendered.

From the moment the titles began, I was completely pulled into the beautiful world of Sita and Ram.

For me, this is one of those rare films where almost every department seems to arrive at the same level at the same time:

Great content. Great casting. Great acting. Great dialogues. Great BGM. Great locations. Great direction. Great production.

That combination is what turns a simple description like “love story” into something much richer.

The writing repeatedly throws up lines and ideas that are meaningful beyond the immediate romance — about helping people beyond the boundaries of “our own,” about the difference between merely carrying a weapon and acting with righteousness, and about how what we believe can sometimes become more powerful than what we actually hear or see.

I especially loved the way Hanu Raghavapudi handles subjects that can easily become politically or emotionally sensitive.

Sumanth’s characterisation is another excellent piece of writing because it brings complexity into a story that could otherwise have become too neatly divided between heroes and villains.

And behind all of this, the production has genuine class.

Swapna Dutt is bringing back the glory associated with her father’s production legacy in terrific style 🙏

I totally loved Sita Ramam.

My kid, of course, had a different verdict: slow, boring and suspiciously lacking in action scenes 😉

But for me — somebody who normally runs away from romantic dramas — this was a CLASSIC and exactly the kind of film I am grateful I watched in a theatre.

e: Vikram is elevated far above its basic drug-mafia story by powerhouse performances and Anirudh’s terrific score. The first half felt confusing and initially made the hype seem excessive, but the way Lokesh Kanagaraj connects the pieces in the second half — and expands the Kaithi universe — is where the film becomes genuinely exciting.
v: Above-average as a standalone drug-mafia film, but much more exciting as the door into Lokesh’s larger universe. Kamal, Fahadh, Vijay Sethupathi and Anirudh do the heavy lifting — and that BGM refuses to leave your head.
body:
For me, Vikram is an above-average drug-mafia movie elevated enormously by its performers and music.

Kamal Haasan, Fahadh Faasil, Vijay Sethupathi and the supporting cast are all top-notch.

And then there is Anirudh’s BGM 🙏🙏🙏

That score stayed in my head even several hours after leaving the theatre.

If I judge Vikram purely as a standalone movie, I would probably call it a one-time watch.

What makes it more interesting is Lokesh Kanagaraj’s larger vision.

The connections to Kaithi and the hints towards future characters give small extra kicks throughout the film and make the universe itself feel larger than this one story.

I only hope future instalments get enough time to fully explore all these characters, because a few of them here feel rushed or not completely justified.

The first half is also a little confusing.

At that stage I honestly wondered whether the enormous hype around the film had oversold it.

But the way the story opens up in the second half is where the director’s planning becomes clear.

Once the pieces begin connecting, much of what initially felt scattered starts making sense.

So while Vikram did not completely blow me away as a standalone film, it absolutely made me interested in the larger world Lokesh is building.

And if you are already a fan of Kaithi, then this becomes a must watch because a big part of the fun lies in seeing those worlds begin to connect.

e: Ante Sundaraniki succeeds at a difficult balance: it tackles sensitive social and family issues without turning into a lecture, while still giving Nani, Nazriya and the ensemble enough comedy to remain a mainstream entertainer. The runtime and music could be tighter, but the writing and performances make it a must watch.
v: Another excellent Vivek Athreya film — funny without diluting its sensitive core, thoughtful without becoming preachy. A little long and musically underpowered, but still a definite MUST WATCH.
body:
Another excellent movie from Vivek Athreya.

When a filmmaker handles a sensitive subject, there is always a very thin line to walk.

Stick too rigidly to the issue and the movie can become preachy and boring.

Add too many commercial elements and the original point gets diluted.

Vivek Athreya and Nani understand that balance very well.

Ante Sundaraniki keeps its core subject alive throughout the film while still finding space for proper entertainment, and it rarely crosses into either extreme.

Nani is completely at home in this world, but the film works because the ensemble around him is equally committed.

Nazriya, Naresh, Rohini, Nadiya, Harshavardhan and the rest of the cast do complete justice to their roles.

The pre-climax and climax are especially effective because all those characters and their conflicting beliefs finally come together in a meaningful way 🙏

If I had one major technical complaint, it would be the music and BGM.

For a film with this much emotional and comic material, the soundtrack should have added far more impact.

And considering how talented Vivek is and how strong this cast is, there is also a lingering feeling that the final result could have been even sharper.

The runtime is definitely debatable; some portions could have been trimmed without losing the heart of the story.

It may not receive the same universal critical love as Mental Madhilo or Brochevarevarura, but for me Ante Sundaraniki is still a MUST WATCH.

e: F3 makes no attempt to disguise what it is: an illogical comedy built around back-to-back episodes rather than a story anyone should analyse seriously. That approach works largely because Venkatesh dominates the film with his comic timing, while Varun Tej, Sunil and Vennela Kishore keep the energy high.
v: More FUN and less FRUSTRATION than F2 😄 Logic can stay outside the theatre — Venky Mama’s comedy timing, Varun Tej, Sunil and Vennela Kishore keep the nonsense entertaining almost all the way through.
body:
Compared with F2, this was more FUN and less FRUSTRATION for me 😄

I am not sure whether the movie itself changed that much or whether I simply entered the theatre better prepared for exactly what Anil Ravipudi was going to serve.

Either way, this time I enjoyed the madness much more.

Once again, it is VENKY MAMA’S SHOW from beginning to end.

Anil Ravipudi knows exactly what an asset Venkatesh’s comedy timing is and uses it to the fullest.

Varun Tej also does a very good job.

In almost any other comedy, this might have been one of his most appreciated performances — but standing next to Venky in this kind of material means getting naturally overshadowed.
