After several attempts, Sunil finally gets a proper full-length comedy role that reminds us of his glorious comic phase.

Then in the second half, even he gets partially pushed aside once Vennela Kishore starts doing what Vennela Kishore does 😄

The best way to approach F3 is the same way you approach franchises such as Golmaal or Housefull.

Nobody is entering the theatre for a carefully constructed story.

You are there to laugh at whatever is happening on screen, even when the scene has no logic and only the loosest connection to the actual plot.

Fortunately, Anil fills the film with enough such episodes to keep the audience entertained.

Once the comedy starts working, you barely notice Devi Sri Prasad’s songs, BGM or many of the other technical departments.

F3 is unapologetically silly cinema — and this time, the silliness worked for me.

e: Sarkaru Vaari Paata starts from a relevant financial theme but loses focus by trying to simultaneously deliver comedy, sentiment, action, hero elevations and message-heavy dialogue. Mahesh Babu carries the film with ease, yet the writing gives him far less than his performance deserves.
v: Strictly average — an interesting, relevant idea buried under commercial mix-and-match. Mahesh is the one real saving grace and repeatedly reminds us how much acting talent is being wasted on formula-heavy message films.
body:
Strictly average.

For me, Sarkaru Vaari Paata is almost entirely Mahesh Babu’s one-man show.

He is the main saving grace 🙏

Audience expectations had started changing rapidly around this period.

After films such as RRR and KGF, a mainstream movie either needed to stay strongly committed to its content, fully embrace its genre, or create such cinematic magic that viewers happily stopped caring about logic.

The old-fashioned commercial formula of mixing a little comedy, sentiment, action, message, romance and heroism into the same pot was becoming much harder to sell.

Parasuram actually chooses an interesting and relevant core point.

Unfortunately, he then weakens it by trying to turn the film into every kind of commercial entertainer at once.

Comedy arrives, then sentiment, then action, then hero elevations, then long dialogues — and the original subject keeps getting lost underneath all that packaging.

The dialogues were a major problem for me.

Several felt irrelevant, lengthy or unnecessarily designed to sound powerful rather than naturally emerging from the scene.

Not every hero can deliver page after page of mass dialogue and make the audience forget what was being discussed in the first place 😄

The most frustrating part is that Mahesh repeatedly shows glimpses of how good an actor he can be.

Those moments make me wish directors would stop trapping him inside silly commercial-message templates and give that talent something genuinely challenging to do.

Sarkaru Vaari Paata had a worthwhile issue at its centre.

It just never trusts that issue enough to build the whole film around it.

e: Acharya is one of those rare Chiranjeevi films that left almost no impression on me at all. Every major selling point had recently been delivered with more impact by another film, while the Chiranjeevi–Ram Charan combination feels driven more by commercial appeal than dramatic necessity.
v: DISASTER!!!! A Chiranjeevi film leaving ZERO impact is almost an achievement by itself. Story, elevations, violence, father-son emotion, music — everything feels like a weaker echo of something we had already seen done better elsewhere.
body:
DISASTER!!!!

When was the last time a Chiranjeevi film left absolutely ZERO impact on me, irrespective of whether it eventually became a hit or flop?

For years my answer was Shankar Dada Zindabad.

Acharya has now taken that position 🙏

The biggest problem is that almost every supposed strength of the film reminded me of something very recent that had already done the same thing with far greater impact.

The story itself did not land because Akhanda had explored similar mass-spiritual territory with much more power.

The violent climax did not shock because Akhanda had already gone further.

The elevation shots did not create a high because audiences were still living in a KGF elevation hangover.

The multistarrer angle did not create an awe factor because RRR had just shown what a major two-star combination could feel like.

Even the father-son attraction of Chiranjeevi and Ram Charan did not generate the emotional novelty it should have; films such as Manam had already shown how powerfully real family relationships can be used on screen.

So the final feeling is simple: there is nothing genuinely new here, and what is being offered is not impactful enough on its own.

The music disappointed me as well.

Lahe Lahe works mainly because of its lyrics, while several other songs sound like they travelled forward from the late ’90s or early 2000s.

And the BGM was so ineffective that I occasionally felt the scenes might have had more impact without it 🤦‍♂️

Ram Charan’s Siddha also feels included more for commercial value than because the story absolutely requires a star of that scale.

I walked out with only one hope:

BOSS, please come back soon.

e: V has the polish expected from Mohana Krishna Indraganti, but never quite finds the extra spark needed to rise above an average-to-good thriller. Nani’s stylish performance and Thaman’s high-octane BGM are the clear highlights, with P. G. Vinda’s cinematography adding plenty of visual flair.
v: Nani’s stylish one-man show with Thaman supplying the real fireworks. An average-to-good thriller that looks slick and sounds terrific, but still leaves you feeling something important is missing.
body:
Nani’s one-man show… with Thaman’s terrific BGM doing serious damage alongside him!

Like several Mohana Krishna Indraganti films, V ultimately settled for me in that average-to-good zone where the craft is visible, the performances are solid, yet you still come away feeling that something is missing.

The biggest strength is clearly Nani.

He gets a stylish part and carries it with complete ease, making the darker shade feel enjoyable even when the material around him is not always giving him enough to work with.

Thaman’s high-octane BGM is the other major asset. It injects energy into the film and gives several scenes more punch than they might have had on paper.

Special mention also to P. G. Vinda’s cinematography and a few stylishly mounted action sequences.

Sudheer Babu, Nivetha Thomas and Aditi Rao Hydari all do their jobs well within the limited scope available to them.

There is nothing disastrously wrong with V, but there is also not enough here to make it truly memorable.

For me, it remains a polished average-to-good watch lifted primarily by Nani’s presence, the visuals and that terrific background score.

e: Uma Maheswara Ugra Roopasya proves how powerful a seemingly simple story can become when every department understands its tone. Venkatesh Maha’s direction, the Araku setting, cinematography, dialogues and Satyadev’s wonderfully subtle performance outweigh the film’s slow pace and less memorable songs.
v: Simple, rooted and beautifully observed. Satyadev is superb, Venkatesh Maha makes the remake feel completely at home in Araku, and a tiny chain of incidents grows into wonderfully satisfying cinema. MUST WATCH.
body:
When an extraordinary director like Venkatesh Maha, a sensible producer like Praveena and an actor as talented as Satyadev came together for a Malayalam remake, my first reaction was honestly: why are these people wasting their talent on a remake?

And then I watched Uma Maheswara Ugra Roopasya.

Man… I got my answer 🙏

I had not watched the Malayalam original at that point, but the film immediately reminded me why Malayalam cinema is so admired for finding extraordinary impact inside incredibly simple situations.

The direction, camera work, locations, dialogues, song lyrics, acting and BGM are all top-notch.

The only negatives I can really point to are the songs themselves and the deliberately slow pace.

Satyadev completely nails the role with a subtle yet deeply effective performance.

There is no unnecessary heroism in the way he plays Mahesh. Every small humiliation, hesitation and emotional shift feels believable.

He is also very well supported by practically every artist around him.

What completely blew me away was the chain of ordinary incidents that eventually leads to the film’s major conflict.

Nothing feels artificially designed as a giant cinematic trigger. One small event leads to another, then another, until suddenly this wonderfully human butterfly effect has changed Mahesh’s life.

That simplicity is the beauty of the writing.

And Venkatesh Maha does not merely remake the material — he makes the world feel completely natural in the Telugu and Araku setting.

For me, this is a MUST WATCH.

e: Lootcase does not need a complicated story or technical fireworks to work. Its biggest strength is the cast — Kunal Kemmu, Rasika Dugal, Vijay Raaz, Ranvir Shorey and Gajraj Rao — who turn a straightforward suitcase comedy into an easy, dependable weekend watch.
v: A simple weekend time-pass powered almost entirely by a terrific comic ensemble. Don’t expect much beyond the laughs — but Kunal Kemmu, Vijay Raaz, Gajraj Rao and gang make sure those laughs keep coming.
body:
A good weekend time-pass.

There is honestly not a great deal to analyse about the story or technical departments of Lootcase.

The entire film works mainly because it has assembled such a talented bunch of performers and then simply allows them to have fun with the material.

Kunal Kemmu, Rasika Dugal, Vijay Raaz, Ranvir Shorey and Gajraj Rao ensure that the movie keeps providing steady entertainment.

Special mention to Vijay Raaz and Gajraj Rao, who are especially enjoyable in their villainous avatars 🙏

The humour comes more from the characters and situations than from any huge plot invention, and that is perfectly fine for the kind of movie this wants to be.

If you simply want to kill some time with a decent comedy, go for it.

It will not disappoint you.

Just do not enter expecting anything much beyond that easy entertainment.

e: Raat Akeli Hai handles murder, abuse and family secrets with far more restraint than its dark premise might suggest. Honey Trehan avoids unnecessary nudity or shock tactics, while the lighting, camera work, Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Radhika Apte create a beautifully moody mystery whose only real drawback is its pace.
v: A dark murder mystery that proves bold content does not need cheap shock value. Vintage-RGV-style lighting, Nawaz and Radhika at their best, and a satisfying final twist make the slow pace easy to forgive.
body:
Raat Akeli Hai is a very well-made murder mystery with a dark underlying subject.

With a title like this, a Netflix release and a story touching on sexual abuse, it would be easy to assume the film will automatically take the no-holds-barred route — cuss words everywhere, nudity, sex and over-the-top violence simply because the platform allows it.

What I liked is that the movie does almost the complete opposite.

The director seems determined to prove that bold content can still be handled cleanly and with restraint.

The subject remains uncomfortable where it needs to be, but the film does not depend on cheap shock value.

The lighting and camera angles throughout the movie repeatedly reminded me of vintage RGV, and I was completely bowled over by that visual mood.

And when you have actors like Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Radhika Apte, you naturally expect strong performances.

They do not disappoint.

The only real negative I can point to is that the film is a little slow.

But that becomes easy to overlook when the performances, atmosphere and final twist are working this well.

For anyone who likes bold content handled with a clean, controlled approach, this is a MUST WATCH.

e: Shakuntala Devi is less interested in explaining how its subject became a mathematical phenomenon than in exploring what happened when an extraordinary personality collided with the expectations of parents, husband and daughter. That choice may disappoint viewers seeking a conventional biopic, but Vidya Balan and Sanya Malhotra make the personal story strongly engaging.
v: Don’t enter expecting a detailed ‘Human Computer’ origin story. As a portrait of a genius struggling with ordinary family relationships, though, it becomes a real treat — powered by effortless Vidya Balan and terrific Sanya Malhotra.
body:
If you are watching Shakuntala Devi expecting a detailed account of the hard work, challenges and effort that turned her into the Human Computer, you may be disappointed.

This is not really that kind of biopic.

Instead, the film is much more interested in the ups and downs of a genius trying to live among ordinary relationships — with her parents, husband and daughter.

And if you approach it from that angle, you are in for a treat.

The director makes that intention clear almost from the first scene itself.

What stayed with me most is the way the film explores a strange contradiction around highly successful people.

Millions of outsiders may admire and celebrate them, yet the people closest to them can experience an entirely different version of the same personality.

That aspect reminded me a little of the emotional conflict in My Father Gandhi.

Vidya Balan absolutely nails the role, as expected.

She moves effortlessly through Shakuntala Devi’s confidence, flamboyance, vulnerability, stubbornness and emotional contradictions.

Sanya Malhotra supports her with a terrific performance and gives the mother-daughter conflict the emotional weight it needs.

Amit Sadh and Jisshu Sengupta have comparatively limited space, but both make their presence felt.

And while plenty of noise is often made about who represents female-centric Hindi cinema, Vidya Balan has quietly been doing that work for years without needing to announce it every time 🙏

So, as a conventional mathematical-genius biopic, Shakuntala Devi may leave some questions unanswered.

As a film about the complicated personal life behind that genius, it worked very well for me.

e: Gulabo Sitabo asks the viewer to adjust to its deliberate pace and strongly local Lucknowi flavour before its pleasures begin to reveal themselves. Once that rhythm clicks, Amitabh Bachchan and Ayushmann Khurrana become two wonderfully petty pillars holding up a sharp landlord-versus-tenant comedy.
v: Patience compulsory 😄 The Lucknowi slang and sloooow narration may test you, but survive that hurdle and Amitabh vs Ayushmann turns a landlord-tenant squabble into a deliciously desi Tom-and-Jerry ride.
body:
You need patience — and a little passion — to enjoy Gulabo Sitabo.

The first hurdle is the strongly Lucknowi dialect.

For a large section of the audience, it may take some time to tune into the language and understand every exchange naturally.

The second hurdle is the sloooow narration 😄

The film is in absolutely no hurry, and that pace can seriously test your patience in the opening stretch.

But if you cross those two barriers, the reward is an excellent little ride powered by Amitabh Bachchan and Ayushmann Khurrana.

Story-wise, it is essentially landlord versus tenant — almost a desi Tom and Jerry setup, only with property, greed and wonderfully petty human behaviour replacing the cartoon traps.

The film also lands a few genuinely good roasts along the way.

On screen, Mirza and Baankey keep trying to outsmart and overshadow one another.

In reality, Amitabh and Ayushmann are doing the exact opposite: they support the story like two major pillars and make the constant bickering enjoyable.

Performances of this level are almost a cakewalk for both of them.

And I do not think I had ever seen Amitabh Bachchan in such a deliciously kameena avatar before 😛

Gulabo Sitabo will definitely not work for everyone.

But if you can surrender to its language, rhythm and deliberately small-scale conflict, there is a lot to enjoy in this strange little battle over an old haveli.

e: Kaamyaab turns the invisible life of Hindi cinema’s character actors into a warm, bittersweet and remarkably restrained film. Sanjay Mishra carries the entire journey with ease, while Hardik Mehta resists melodrama and lets the final irony — that even the finest sidekick remains overshadowed by the hero — land naturally.
v: A beautifully simple salute to the faces we all recognise but rarely remember by name. No melodrama, no commercial decoration — just Sanjay Mishra carrying a painfully real story to a wonderfully written climax. MUST WATCH.
body:
If you are open to a non-commercial film with a simple storyline and excellent performances, Kaamyaab is a MUST WATCH.

In roughly an hour and a half, the movie gives us a glimpse into the lives of the countless character actors and sidekicks who have appeared in hundreds of Hindi films without ever becoming household names.

We know their faces.

We have seen them as smugglers, policemen, doctors, villains, henchmen and fathers.

Yet many of us would struggle to name them.

There is something both funny and sad about the fact that the age of social media can suddenly make these forgotten performers recognisable again because one expression or scene becomes a meme.

Kaamyaab understands that strange afterlife beautifully.

Sanjay Mishra is terrific and carries the entire film on his shoulders.

The role fits his ability to make an ordinary man’s smallest disappointment feel completely real.

What I appreciated just as much is that director Hardik Mehta never tries to force melodrama into the story.

The world remains grounded and believable throughout.

Even the climax is written with wonderful restraint.

The final idea is both simple and painful: no matter how well a side actor performs, and no matter how much the audience enjoys him, the spotlight will almost always move back towards the HERO.

That is what makes Kaamyaab more than merely a film-industry story.

It is a heartfelt salute to generations of performers who helped make our movies memorable while remaining almost invisible themselves 🙏

e: Shubh Mangal Zyada Saavdhan deliberately treats its same-sex romance like the most ordinary Bollywood family conflict possible. That simplicity is both its strength and limitation: the film never becomes a hard-hitting message drama or an all-out comedy, but Ayushmann, Jitendra and the ensemble make a still-taboo subject accessible without melodrama.
v: A very familiar family-love-story template with one important difference: the couple happens to be two men. It sits awkwardly between message movie and full comedy, but the cast makes the subject feel refreshingly normal and easy to watch.
body:
MAN!!! Is there any genre Ayushmann Khurrana cannot do with ease?

Story-wise, Shubh Mangal Zyada Saavdhan is actually a very familiar Bollywood love story.

Two people fall in love.

The family does not approve.

In the second half, one partner enters the other partner’s family world and tries to win everybody over.

Eventually we move towards the classic “Jaa Simran jaa… jee le apni zindagi” territory 😄

The major difference, of course, is that the lead pair are two men.

Writer-director Hitesh Kewalya makes an interesting choice with that subject.

He does not turn homosexuality into a heavy melodramatic issue packed with giant message dialogues.

But he also does not make the movie an out-and-out family comedy in the way something like Dream Girl was.

As a result, the film lands somewhere in between.

It is neither a powerful message-oriented drama nor a complete laugh riot.

That middle ground limits the impact a little for me.

At the same time, the approach has one major advantage: the relationship itself begins to feel wonderfully normal.

All the actors are very good, and the characterisations help make a subject that was still treated as taboo by many viewers feel simple and watchable even for a mainstream family audience.

That normalisation may actually be more useful than repeatedly announcing the film’s social importance.

So do not enter expecting too much from the plot or comedy and you are likely to enjoy it.

And for those of us who have spent years thumping our chests about Ayushmann’s script choices… yes, he gives us one more film to brag about 😄

e: Bheeshma uses organic farming as its plot foundation but Venky Kudumula keeps the message secondary to entertainment. The first half is okay, the post-interval comedy lifts the film considerably, and Nithiin, Vennela Kishore, Raghu Babu and the stylish presentation make it an easy commercial watch if you leave logic at the door.
v: Nithiin is back on the HIT track! The organic-farming message takes a back seat to comedy, but once the second half lets loose, the punches and performances make this a pakka commercial entertainer.
body:
Nithiin is back again on the HIT track!!!

Plot-wise, the concept of organic farming is almost kicked aside by director Venky Kudumula’s narration style.

It is interesting how differently directors can approach the same kind of subject. If this plot had been handled by someone like Koratala Siva, it could easily have become a commercially serious, message-oriented film with stylish action scenes. Venky chooses a completely different route and mixes entertainment into the message-heavy setup.

The message is almost dominated by the comedy, but for a general entertainment-loving audience that is not necessarily a bad thing.

The first half was okay. With the interval twist, I actually thought the second half would turn serious and that all the hype about the comedy was going to be a bluff.

But the immediate post-interval scene makes the director’s intention very clear — he is not leaving the comedy angle at all — and that is where the real fun starts!!!!!

The one-liners, punches and even those intentionally irritating meme-style lines given to Nithiin are well written. Raghu Babu and Vennela Kishore together rock to the core!!!!

The movie is also shot quite stylishly. The BGM works, there are a couple of hit songs and the fights are good.

Surprisingly, the songs do not give Nithiin too many chances to show off his dancing, and in the only proper mass number Rashmika ends up taking most of the attention 😄

Overall, this is a pakka commercial entertainer with plenty of comedy in the second half, where the hero can happily do all the buffoonery and still remain the HERO!!!

Do not enter expecting a serious message or too much logic, and you are likely to enjoy it.

e: Panga takes a story that could easily have been pushed into loud melodrama and tells it with wonderful simplicity and realism instead. Ashwiny Iyer Tiwari gets the emotions right, Kangana Ranaut is superb, and the entire supporting cast helps turn it into an effortless must-watch.
v: Excellent!!!!! Simple, realistic and refreshingly free of melodrama. Kangana is superb, the supporting cast clicks, and this is a MUST WATCH — theatre or OTT, the sooner the better!!!
body:
Excellent!!!!!

How do you make a movie with this kind of story in such a simple and realistic way, without falling into unnecessary melodrama?

For me, there was hardly a scene that felt unrealistic. Director Ashwiny Iyer Tiwari does a fantastic job of getting the emotions right without forcing them.

We already know Kangana Ranaut is a fantastic and natural actor, but man, she is a SUPER STAR 🙏

She portrays all the emotions of a housewife carrying an unfinished dream in a wonderfully natural way.

And it is not just Kangana. Jassie Gill, Richa Chadha and Neena Gupta all do their jobs perfectly.

Special mention also to the kid playing the son — he fits into the family beautifully and adds a lot of warmth to the film.

The music and BGM blend perfectly with the mood, while the dialogues stay simple yet make complete sense.

Whether you watch it in a theatre or later on OTT, this is a MUST WATCH.

The sooner, the better!!!

e: Disco Raja throws sci-fi, retro styling and regular mass cinema into the same mixer, but Vi Anand never fully balances the concept with Ravi Teja’s trademark energy. There are interesting ingredients — especially Sunil’s return and Thaman’s terrific music and BGM — yet the film ultimately lands only a little above average.
v: Neither good nor bad — just above average. The sci-fi idea, retro setup, Sunil and Thaman create interest, but Ravi Teja’s energy overwhelms the concept until the film starts feeling routine.
body:
Personally, I feel Disco Raja is almost Vi Anand’s version of iSmart Shankar — sci-fi and regular mass cinema thrown together into one mixer!!!!!

The biggest challenge with Ravi Teja is that a director has to decide how much to use his energy levels and comedy timing.

If you do not use them enough, a section of the audience may feel the movie is slow and dull.

But if you use them too much, Ravi Teja can take over the entire film with his high energy and push the concept and story into the background.

And that is where I felt Vi Anand failed to find the right balance.

The sci-fi concept, the retro setup and the re-introduction of Sunil all create genuine interest.

But once Ravi Teja arrives in full Disco Raja mode, his energy overshadows almost everything around him, and that is when the movie starts feeling routine despite the unusual setup.

Apart from Ravi Teja, the two things that grabbed my attention most were Thaman’s terrific music and BGM and Sunil 🙏

There is enough style and novelty in the ingredients to keep it from becoming a bad film, but the execution never turns those ingredients into something truly special.

Overall, it is neither a good nor a bad movie — just above average!!!

e: Ala Vaikunthapurramuloo reveals its basic story almost immediately, yet Trivikram keeps the film engaging through comedy, family emotions and strong character work. Allu Arjun gets a full showcase, Murali Sharma is a terrific second pillar, and Thaman’s chartbusters and BGM give this simple commercial film plenty of life.
v: A wafer-thin, predictable family story that I still liked to the core! Trivikram’s comedy and emotions, Allu Arjun, Murali Sharma and Thaman turn it into a simple, cool entertainer.
body:
Very rarely do you see a film where you cannot point to one single outstanding element, yet you still like the film to the core — a little like Seethamma Vakitlo Sirimalle Chettu for me.

Ala Vaikunthapurramuloo falls into that category.

You can understand the basic story within the first ten minutes, but Trivikram’s command over comedy and family emotions, Murali Sharma’s excellent characterisation and acting, and Allu Arjun’s all-round performance keep you engaged for the entire length.

Because the family story itself is wafer-thin, Trivikram does not get as much space to show the kind of intellectual dialogue brilliance we saw in films such as Aravinda Sametha, Julayi or Khaleja.

Even then, his pen keeps moving, with a few trademark Trivikram lines scattered throughout the film.

Allu Arjun is back with a bang!!!

He gets a brilliant opportunity to handle comedy, emotion, mass fights and class fights in a single movie. And once again, he proves why he is among the best dancers in Tollywood — those trademark graceful steps look simple until you imagine trying to perform them yourself 🙏

Special mention to the dance episode in the office boardroom. It creates the kind of instant crowd impact that reminded me of Gabbar Singh’s antakshari scene, while cleverly giving PK fans their little ego-satisfaction moment too 😄

Trivikram and the fight masters also make sure the action portions are staged with conviction.

And unlike Agnyaathavaasi and Aravinda Sametha, this time Trivikram takes extra care not to spoil the impact of the chartbuster songs with their picturisation. The lead-in scenes, locations and sets blend nicely with the songs.

On screen, if Allu Arjun is one pillar, Murali Sharma is the other.

His characterisation and performance create exactly the impact required for us to dislike him throughout the film.

Apart from Murali Sharma and Sachin Khedekar, though, many of the other star actors are used more or less like junior artists 😦

Thaman gives the movie enormous life with his chartbuster songs and ultra-cool BGM.

Overall, this is a simple, cool commercial film that worked very well for me, especially as an Allu Arjun and Murali Sharma showcase.

The story may be familiar and predictable, but the entertainment around it makes the ride worthwhile.

e: Sarileru Neekevvaru finally lets Mahesh Babu step away from his recent message-heavy films and enjoy a full mass avatar. His comedy timing, punch dialogues and screen presence are refreshing, but an overdone train episode, thin content and a weak, illogical climax make the overall experience much more mixed for a neutral audience.
v: Babu neee Maaassu… Mind Blocku!!! Mahesh’s mass comeback is a treat for fans, but for neutral viewers the silly train comedy and weak climax keep it only a time-pass average entertainer.
body:
Babu neee Maaassu… Bomma Mind Blocku!!!!!

For Mahesh Babu fans, Sarileru Neekevvaru is almost what Gabbar Singh was for Pawan Kalyan fans — they are going to enjoy this mass avatar of MB to the core.

For a neutral audience, though, it is more of a time-pass average movie.

I had honestly become a little tired of Mahesh’s seemingly endless run of message-oriented and family films over the previous few years, especially with the similar performance style and sloooww dialogue modulation.

So this movie felt like fresh air simply because it finally explores his mass-entertainer potential again.

And Mahesh completely owns that space.

His trademark comedy timing works, the punchy dialogues suit him, and his dance and grace in the Mind Block song are going to be a proper treat for fans.

Content-wise, there is nothing particularly new here. It follows the familiar mass-film template, but because Mahesh returns to this genre after such a looooong gap, even familiar material feels a little refreshing.

Director Anil Ravipudi seems determined to live up to expectations around his comedy track, and unfortunately that makes him overdo it.

The entire train episode is packed with exaggerated performances from Sangeetha, Rashmika and others.

A certain section of the audience may get irritated with that never-ending silliness — I certainly did 😄 — while people who love this kind of masssss comedy may enjoy it completely.

My daughter was laughing out loud through that whole sequence while I was sitting there wondering when it would finally end, so that probably explains the divide perfectly.

The climax tries to be different, but it is very weak and illogical even by mass-movie standards.

On the positive side, the confrontation scenes involving Prakash Raj, Vijayashanti and Mahesh in the second half are handled superbly, mixing powerful punches with comedy nicely.

DSP’s music is quite ordinary, though the songs are shot well. The BGM is much better and gives the hero-elevation moments exactly the lift they need.

Overall, this feels designed to be a runaway entertainer in B and C centres, where the complete mass package will probably work extremely well.

For audiences expecting stronger content, subtler comedy or a sensible climax, the experience is likely to stay much closer to average.

e: Chhapaak worked for me because Meghna Gulzar treats an extremely painful subject with restraint. The film explores not just an acid-attack survivor’s struggle but also family support, women’s empowerment and the exhausting reality of sustaining a social cause, with Deepika Padukone and Vikrant Massey carrying the emotions without unnecessary drama.
v: Not for the regular moviegoer, but absolutely a MUST WATCH. Meghna Gulzar keeps the pain, dignity and message simple and effective instead of turning an acid-attack survivor’s story into melodrama.
body:
Not for the regular moviegoer… but a MUST WATCH!!!

Meghna Gulzar brilliantly shows the struggles faced by an acid-attack survivor and her family without reducing the subject to one-note suffering.

The film also brings in women’s empowerment and the constant practical struggle involved in running — and financially sustaining — a social cause.

There were a few things I especially loved.

The relationship between the lawyer and her husband is handled beautifully.

There are no giant dialogues or dramatic declarations around his support, yet the film quietly shows how a husband can help his wife chase her dreams by simply getting involved in the basic, everyday things that make those dreams possible 🙏

I also liked the sweet relationship between Amol and Malti.

Personally, I would probably have preferred them to remain friends rather than moving towards romance, but since the film draws from a real-life story, there is not much to argue about there 😄

The lyrics are excellent and the music stays simple, allowing us to feel the pain of acid-attack victims without forcing emotion through loud filmmaking.

The dialogues follow the same approach — simple, effective and never overloaded with drama, yet they still communicate the pain and the message clearly.

Performance-wise, Deepika Padukone has already proved herself many times, so I would not say the acting challenge itself is the surprising part here.

What deserves appreciation is her decision to take up a film like this, because her presence allows the subject to reach a much wider audience.

Vikrant Massey also does a very good job as Amol, particularly in showing the emotions of someone who is deeply committed to a cause but is constantly struggling with the reality of being able to afford that commitment.

Chhapaak is not an easy entertainment watch, and it is not trying to be one.

But for the subject it takes on, and the restraint with which it communicates that subject, it is absolutely worth watching.

e: Darbar gives Rajinikanth plenty of chances to remind us why his style remains unmatched, and Anirudh’s BGM amplifies those moments wonderfully. But the writing feels badly dated, the logic is often baffling and Murugadoss never builds enough around that star power, leaving only scattered fan moments in an otherwise disappointing film.
v: Rajini’s style plus Anirudh’s BGM can still touch the sky — unfortunately Darbar’s positives pretty much end there. Outdated writing and baffling logic waste the Superstar’s screen presence.
body:
Many actors have tried to imitate his style and grace, and Rajinikanth himself has done these gestures a zillion times — yet somehow it is still a treat to watch Thalaivaa’s STYLE!!!

Darbar once again proves that he is the one and only STYLE ICON.

And when Rajini’s style meets Anirudh’s BGM, only the sky is the limit!!!!!

Unfortunately, Darbar’s positives more or less end there.

Was this really written and directed by A.R. Murugadoss?

Man, how could he make a movie filled with material that feels this outdated 😦

I already felt he had lost some form after Spyder — even though I personally liked that film for its different concept — but Darbar made that concern much stronger.

Some of the writing and logic are genuinely baffling.

There is even a scene where the backstory says a father was killed roughly twenty-seven years earlier, while in the present a four- or five-year-old child is shown kissing his photograph and saying, “Miss you, Dad.”

How does that timeline even work? 🙏

Beyond Rajini’s presence and the BGM, there is honestly not much else I felt strongly about.

Anirudh’s background score is excellent, but the songs are almost equally disappointing.

Fans who simply want to enjoy Rajini’s style may find a few portions worth cheering for.

Fans expecting a strong Murugadoss film, though, are probably better off staying away.

The frustrating part is that Rajini still has enormous screen presence, yet the current lot of filmmakers rarely seem to use it fully enough to create the kind of impact we saw in films like Narasimha.

That wasted potential is what makes Darbar more disappointing than merely routine.

e: Prathi Roju Pandage feels extremely familiar in both story and treatment, with Maruthi’s humour and Raashi Khanna’s TikTok-obsessed character providing most of the variation. The real reason to watch is Rao Ramesh, who carries the routine family drama so completely that Sai Dharam Tej can sometimes feel like he is appearing in an extended cameo.
v: A routine family-values drama that often feels like Shatamanam Bhavati revisited — but Rao Ramesh almost single-handedly turns hero, villain and comedian and keeps the film alive.
body:
Story-wise, Prathi Roju Pandage almost felt like a sequel to Shatamanam Bhavati, and even much of the treatment reminded me of the same film.

Director Maruthi adds his trademark humour and gives the heroine the gimmick of being a TikTok addict, but apart from those touches there is very little here that feels different from the many recent so-called family-values movies.

The one person who completely lifts this otherwise routine family drama is Rao Ramesh.

He carries the film on his shoulders so comfortably that after a few scenes you genuinely start feeling that he — and only he — is the HERO, VILLAIN and COMEDIAN of the movie!!!!!

Raashi Khanna does a good job as the TikTok queen, while the rest of the family characters support Rao Ramesh’s terrific performance well.

Sai Dharam Tej, surprisingly, almost feels like he has an extended-cameo kind of role in comparison.

He does a decent job with what he is given, but the movie never really feels like it belongs to him.

There is not much to say about the remaining departments because none of them are particularly bad, but none of them stand out as exceptional either.

Overall, it is a familiar and fairly average family entertainer whose biggest strength is one performer making routine material much more watchable than it might otherwise have been.

e: Amma Rajyam Lo Kadapa Biddalu felt less like a movie and more like a long political spoof designed to ridicule a few people while glorifying another. The uncanny casting, makeup and imitations are genuinely impressive, but beyond that I found almost no story, emotion or entertainment to hold onto.
v: Terrific casting and makeup cannot rescue a film built almost entirely around mocking real people. RGV himself says audiences want entertainment — this is miles away from providing it.
body:
I generally try to watch a movie simply as a movie and nothing else.

But here it was crystal clear to me that the entire exercise was created mainly to make a mockery of a few people and project one person as the greatest leader.

I had liked Lakshmi’s NTR because, irrespective of whom it was targeting politically, there was still a human story underneath it.

At its centre was the relationship between an aged, lonely man and an already-married woman, along with the consequences they faced because that man belonged to one of the most powerful political families.

There was something to engage with beyond the attack itself.

In Amma Rajyam Lo Kadapa Biddalu, I could not find that layer.

Most of the film felt like one spoof after another, with the audience simply being asked to recognise the real-life personalities being mocked.

The one department I genuinely appreciated was the casting and makeup.

The team does terrific work in making several actors resemble the personalities they are imitating, and the versions of Lokesh, Pawan Kalyan and K.A. Paul come surprisingly close in appearance and mannerisms.

But accurate imitation alone cannot carry an entire film.

RGV himself has a line in the movie saying that whether it is politics, cinema or life, the audience ultimately expects entertainment.

By that standard, this film fails its own argument.

For a general audience looking for an actual movie rather than a collection of political spoofs, it is far, far away from providing any real entertainment.

e: Venky Mama survives almost entirely on Venkatesh’s effortless comedy and emotional timing and the chemistry between the uncle and nephew. The story, dialogue, direction, music and BGM leave little impression, while the pre-climax and climax become so illogical that even Venky’s charm cannot fully save the film.
v: As the title suggests, it is Venky’s one-man show. His comedy, emotion and mama-alludu chemistry are the only real saving grace in an otherwise below-par film with a patience-testing climax.
body:
As the title itself suggests, this is Venky’s one-man show!!!

His comedy timing, emotional timing and the mama-alludu chemistry are easily the best things in the film.

Unfortunately, once you move beyond those elements, there is not much to say about the story, dialogues, direction, BGM or music.

None of those departments gives the film enough strength or identity of its own.

The pre-climax and climax are especially frustrating.

They stretch the audience’s patience with sequences that become completely illogical 🙏

Venkatesh keeps trying to lift the material through sheer warmth, timing and screen presence, and whenever he is in control the movie becomes noticeably more watchable.

But one performer can carry only so much.

Venky Mama himself is the saving grace for an otherwise below-par film.

e: Housefull 4 knows exactly what kind of movie it wants to be: loud, illogical and proudly ridiculous. It is neither the best nor the worst of the franchise, but Akshay Kumar’s expressions, the ensemble madness and a stream of absurd surprises made it a thoroughly enjoyable time-pass watch for me.
v: LOVED IT!!!!!! Leave logic, emotion and message at home and this becomes a proper mad laugh riot. Akshay steals the show, even if my beloved Aakhri Pasta deserved much better 😄
body:
LOVED IT!!!!!!

If you want a fun-filled, crazy movie and are completely willing to forget logic, this is exactly the kind of film that can work.

If you are going in expecting logic, deep emotions and a message… please stay at home 😄

I have followed both the Golmaal and Housefull franchises for years, and I would not call this the best entry in the series.

But it is definitely not the worst either.

Akshay Kumar is the real all-rounder of Bollywood.

He can move from action films to national-integrity dramas, message-oriented cinema and then jump straight into the complete madness of Housefull without looking uncomfortable for a second.

Here he steals the show with those epic facial expressions.

It also takes a certain confidence for a major star to accept a character that functions more like the film’s main comedian than a conventional HERO, and Akshay commits fully to the madness.

As a big fan of Aakhri Pasta, though, I was disappointed that the character was not etched as memorably as in the earlier Housefull films.

That was probably my biggest personal disappointment.

Beyond that, the film keeps throwing ridiculous surprises at you — including Nawazuddin Siddiqui turning up in an ITEM SONG and Hulk Rana becoming qawwali singer Rangeela Raja 🙏

Nothing here should be examined too seriously.

Overall, it is a nice time-pass laugh riot if you can surrender to the illogical plot and completely mad comedy!!!!!

e: Sye Raa starts with a very familiar patriotic-film template and spends too long on family and romance, but the movie changes dramatically once its central conflict takes over. From there, Chiranjeevi, the huge supporting cast and the technical departments combine to deliver the scale, intensity and fan moments the opening stretch was missing.
v: The first 45 minutes are painful and familiar, but once the revolt begins Sye Raa transforms into a BLOCKBUSTER ride — Chiru’s eyes, dialogue diction and final stretch make the dream project come alive.
body:
To start with, Sye Raa follows a very familiar patriotic-film structure.

Character introduction and early life, followed by oppression, revolt, backstabbing and then the end — the broad screenplay beats are all very recognisable.

To make matters worse, the first forty-five minutes were honestly painful for me.

There is too much focus on Narasimha Reddy’s family and romance, and the Chiranjeevi–Nayanthara–Tamannaah portions did not convince me at all.

But what follows that difficult opening stretch is what turns the movie around completely.

Once the central conflict is firmly established, Sye Raa becomes a BLOCKBUSTER experience.

From that point onwards it is a treat to watch the effort put in by the director, fight masters, dialogue writers, DOP and music team 🙏

A cast containing Chiranjeevi, Amitabh Bachchan, Kiccha Sudeep, Jagapathi Babu and Ravi Kishan gives the film enormous screen presence and helps carry the required intensity.

Yes, it can initially be difficult to imagine a sixty-plus Chiranjeevi physically as this warrior.

But then you look at the INTENSITY in his eyes and listen to the diction in those dialogues, and he convinces you to stop thinking about his age.

Acting-wise, for me this is among his best performances since Apadbandhavudu!!!!!

Surender Reddy’s direction becomes very strong once the story enters its main conflict, and he understands exactly when to give Chiru fans those big moments.

Special mention to the final ten minutes, which showcase Chiranjeevi’s intensity to the core 🙏

It was also good to finally see Tamannaah and Kiccha Sudeep receive substantial roles.

Tamannaah does very well, while Sudeep is excellent — he owns several scenes with that wonderfully careless attitude and at times even manages to dominate the frame opposite Chiru.

I was disappointed that Vijay Sethupathi was limited to only a couple of scenes because there was barely enough room for him to show what he can really do, although his screen presence still adds value.

Amitabh’s role is far more subtle as the guru.

But when performers of this calibre fill the screen together, it is simply an awesome sight.

In the end, the actors and technicians clearly put enormous effort into making Chiranjeevi’s dream project a SUCCESS.

If the opening forty-five minutes had been as strong as what follows, the impact could have been even bigger.

e: GangLeader suffers mainly from the huge expectations created by Vikram Kumar and Nani joining hands. Taken on its own terms, though, the deliberately ordinary heroes and villain, subtle comedy and a handful of wonderfully staged scenes make the simple revenge story feel far more distinctive than its plot suggests.
v: Personally, I LOVED it!!! A simple revenge story gets Vikram Kumar’s special treatment, with Nani at his natural best and enough clever framing to reward viewers who enjoy something different.
body:
Personally, I loved the movie!!!

This time Vikram Kumar takes a simple revenge story and gives it his own special treatment.

There are about five scenes in particular — the opening, the interval framing, two moments in the second half and the post-climax reveal involving Sravani’s character — that really show the intelligence of the director 🙏

The biggest setback for the film is probably not the film itself, but the expectations surrounding it.

After Manam, and with a combination like Vikram Kumar and Nani, audiences naturally walk in expecting a highly intelligent and hugely entertaining thriller.

If you remove that burden and simply watch what is on screen, there is a lot to appreciate.

One of Vikram’s interesting choices is that none of the main characters is conventionally powerful — not even the villain.

That can be difficult for a regular audience used to the larger-than-life heroes and intimidating villains of Rajamouli- or Boyapati-style cinema.

But that lack of exaggerated power is also what gives this story its own flavour.

Nani is, as usual, at his natural best and completely submits himself to the character rather than trying to turn it into another star vehicle.

Anirudh’s BGM is trendy and works nicely with the mood, although I expected stronger songs from someone of his calibre.

Even with simple characters, a deliberately understated villain and fairly subtle comedy, the film manages to keep a grip on the audience.

This is strictly not for viewers looking for a powerful hero-villain clash or a full-length Nani comedy entertainer.

But audiences who enjoy slightly different genre films are much more likely to connect with what Vikram is trying to do here.

e: Chhichhore captures college friendships with characters who feel instantly familiar, then blends that nostalgia with a genuinely meaningful emotional message. Nitesh Tiwari and his writers balance comedy, sentiment and emotion in almost perfect proportions, creating the rare film whose effort and result are both complete successes.
v: Man!!!! What a movie. Chhichhore deserves to sit beside Dil Chahta Hai, 3 Idiots and Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara — hilarious, emotional, wonderfully real and carrying a message that actually stays with you.
body:
Man!!!! What a movie…

I am not exaggerating when I say Chhichhore has what it takes to sit in the same conversation as films like Dil Chahta Hai, 3 Idiots and Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara.

It has shades of all three, but it still stands on its own because of the emotional message it delivers and the wonderfully realistic way it portrays college life and friendships.

Almost every group of friends can identify an Anni, Sexa, Acid, Mummy or Bevda somewhere in its own history 😄

That familiarity makes the humour work even before the larger emotional story takes over.

Director Nitesh Tiwari and his team of writers do a fantastic job with the story, dialogues and screenplay.

Emotion, sentiment and comedy are mixed in almost perfect proportions.

The screenplay is especially strong because the film can move between laughter and pain without making either side feel artificial.

You come away feeling as though you watched an emotional comedy, a friendship film and a message-oriented drama at the same time — without any one ingredient crushing the others.

One line in the film essentially sums up the entire idea: your result does not decide whether you are a success or a failure; your effort does.

And in my view, the Chhichhore team succeeds on both counts.

They clearly put in the effort — and the result is outstanding too 🙏

e: Dream Girl takes a premise that could easily have slipped into cheap or vulgar comedy and handles it with surprising control. Ayushmann is effortlessly convincing, Raaj Shaandilyaa’s writing keeps the jokes lively without crossing the line, and the supporting cast turns the unusual setup into a bright, accessible entertainer.
v: Where does Ayushmann get the guts to keep picking these subjects? 😄 Raaj Shaandilyaa keeps the comedy spicy and witty without letting it become vulgar, while a terrific supporting cast sells every bit of the madness.
body:
Where does Ayushmann Khurrana get the guts to keep selecting such unconventional subjects — and then perform them so naturally and convincingly?!!!!!

He really does look like he is on the path to becoming one of Bollywood’s next big performers alongside Rajkummar Rao.

Story-wise, I felt the basic idea had a little flavour of Tumhari Sulu, except with Ayushmann effectively becoming the Pooja voice at the centre of the chaos.

This is also exactly the kind of premise that could have gone badly wrong.

If handled without control, the so-called decent family audience could easily have rejected it as vulgar comedy.

That is where debut director and writer Raaj Shaandilyaa shows his experience and talent.

The dialogues remain spicy and witty enough to keep the comedy alive, but they rarely cross the border into being unnecessarily vulgar.

Another masterstroke is the supporting cast.

The film surrounds Ayushmann with strong comic performers who understand how to deliver this material with exactly the right tone — naughty enough to be funny, but controlled enough to remain broadly watchable.

The BGM complements the mood very well, the couple of major songs fit the content nicely and the visuals stay bright and appealing.

The one drawback, if I have to pick one, is the heavy use of Haryanvi and Uttar Pradesh slang.

It gives the setting a much more realistic flavour, but audiences from other parts of the country may need a little extra effort to catch every line and enjoy the comedy as effortlessly as local viewers.

That is a relatively small limitation in an otherwise smartly handled and very entertaining comedy.

e: iSmart Shankar is Puri Jagannadh going back to unapologetic mass cinema, this time with a sci-fi hook and Ram operating at absurd energy levels. The writing may not have Puri’s hardest-hitting dialogue, but Mani Sharma’s BGM, Ram’s performance and the director’s full-throttle attitude made this exactly the kind of mass feast I wanted.
v: When three baaaps of MASS — Puri, Mani and Ram — come together, the result is an Isssssmartish BLOCKBUSTER! Sci-fi backdrop, full mass kick, Mani’s BGM and Ram’s mad energy… poyiiii kummundri!!!!!
body:
When three baaaps of MASS — Puri, Mani and Ram — come together… the result is an Isssssmartish BLOCKBUSTER 🙏

Puri Jagannadh chooses a completely massssssy movie with a sci-fi backdrop and, mannnn, he delivers!!!!!!

Being a Puriiii fan, I have enjoyed most of his earlier work, and this movie was no different for me.

If anything, Puri makes sure to add an extra dose of mass kick this time.

Dialogue-wise, this may not contain the kind of hard-hitting lines we associate with Puri at his very best, but he still throws in a few excellent mass dialogues at exactly the right moments.

Mani Sharma’s BGM is superb.

The climax score in particular gives you that instant HIGH the moment it kicks in!!!!!

And then there is Ram 🙏🙏

At times I genuinely wondered what he had taken to produce such a hyper-energetic performance 😄

He throws himself into the body language, slang and madness with zero hesitation.

Finally… aaadaaa Puri, Mani & Ram kalisi balisina potellani kosi… garam masala poosiiii… masth biryaniiii vandaaru!!!!!

Poyiiiii kummundri!!!!! 🔥

e: Falaknuma Das has a few actors doing genuinely good work, but their effort disappears inside a 150-minute film that felt painfully stretched and repetitive. I am normally open to realistic cinema, but here the refusal to use emotion, twists or entertainment made the so-called realism feel more like a test of patience than a strength.
v: One of the worst movies I had seen after Brahmotsavam — a short-film-sized story stretched endlessly in the name of realism until patience itself becomes the real victim.
body:
One of the worst movies I had seen after Brahmotsavam!!!!!

The basic storyline felt like something that could comfortably have worked as a twenty-minute short film.

Instead, it is stretched… stretched… and stretched into roughly 150 minutes.

For me, Falaknuma Das became an example of how badly an audience’s patience can be tested when a filmmaker becomes so committed to a so-called realistic approach that he refuses almost every bit of cinematic liberty.

There is barely any attempt to build stronger emotion, twists or entertainment around the story.

A few actors perform very well, and that deserves acknowledgment.

Unfortunately, their efforts are wasted because we keep returning to the same far-stretched, repetitive scenes without enough purpose or progression.

I am generally open to different genres and to realistic films.

So my problem is not realism itself.

The problem is that here I could see almost nothing beyond the director’s determination to make a realistic film with a realistic story, realistic emotions and realistic dialogues — even when that realism was doing very little to keep the movie engaging.

For a normal moviegoer, this can become extremely frustrating.

For me, it was a total waste of time!!!!!

e: Jersey is unapologetically emotional rather than mass entertainment, so its impact depends heavily on what kind of cinema you enjoy. For viewers who connect with realistic drama, Nani’s effortless performance, Gowtam Tinnanuri’s direction, well-shot cricket scenes and touching dialogues make it a deeply rewarding watch.
v: REEListic story dealt with REAListic emotions! A must-watch for emotional-content lovers, with Nani making an award-worthy role look like a cakewalk and the cricket portions landing beautifully.
body:
REEListic story dealt with REAListic emotions!!!!

If you are a fan of movies driven by emotional content, Jersey is a must watch.

If you are a regular movie lover, it is still worth a one-time watch.

And if you watch cinema purely for mass entertainment, then this may simply not be your kind of film.

What could have become an award-winning, once-in-a-lifetime performance for many actors feels almost like a cakewalk for Nani.

He makes the frustration, vulnerability and determination of the character feel completely natural.

Director Gowtam Tinnanuri does full justice to the emotional theme, and the cricket portions are also shot really well.

The songs themselves are fairly ordinary, but the BGM is much better.

It stays relatively subtle and still manages to elevate the emotional mood whenever required.

Shraddha Srinath, Sathyaraj and the little kid all do complete justice to their respective roles.

Special mention also goes to the dialogues.

They often sound conversational rather than manufactured, and several lines carry the pain of the character without needing theatrical presentation.

One of the strongest ideas in the film is that success is not merely about talent; sometimes it is about the ability to keep trying even when everyone around you has quietly stopped expecting anything from you.

That combination of cricket, failure, family and self-respect is what made Jersey work for me.

e: F2 reminded me of the old family multi-starrers where frustrated husbands run away from domestic life, get into trouble and eventually rediscover the value of family. Anil Ravipudi revives that template with plenty of loud comedy, but almost everything irritated me except Venkatesh slipping comfortably back into his vintage comic zone.
v: I felt more FRUSTRATION than Fun. The story, silly comedy, songs and overacting exhausted me; the one genuine pleasure is watching vintage Venky return to comedy after a long gap.
body:
I felt FRUSTRATED more than I felt any Fun!!!!

Back in the late 1990s and early 2000s, there was a phase of so-called family multi-starrers where a group of husbands or friends became fed up with their wives and families, wandered onto the wrong path and eventually realised the importance of marriage and family.

Movies like Sandade Sandadi and Kshemanga Velli Labhanga Randi wrapped that basic idea in endless, often mindless comedy.

They also tended to feature a familiar combination of established or fading stars, struggling younger heroes and dependable comedy performers such as Rajendra Prasad.

Anil Ravipudi seems heavily inspired by that golden era here — only this time he brings together Venkatesh, Varun Tej and, once again, Mr. Rajendra Prasad.

Unfortunately, almost every major ingredient frustrated me.

The story was frustrating.

The silly comedy was frustrating.

The songs and BGM were frustrating.

The family drama was frustrating.

And the heroines and Prakash Raj are pushed into such exaggerated performances that even they became frustrating.

The one genuine FUN for me was watching vintage Venky return to a full comedy movie after a long gap.

His timing still works, and whenever he gets space to play, you get a glimpse of why he was so comfortable in this genre for years.

But that alone was not enough to rescue the movie for me.

e: Vinaya Vidheya Rama takes every familiar Boyapati ingredient and pushes it several levels beyond excess: more emotion, more villainy, louder dialogues, bigger fights and logic that disappears almost completely. Ram Charan’s ease with the high-voltage material is the only real positive I found, even though my daughter apparently had a very different verdict 😄
v: Boyapati’s regular mass template gets turned past OVER-the-top — family, villain, fights, dialogues and even physics go berserk. Ram Charan is the lone positive, comfortably surviving the madness.
body:
Ram Charan did a Balakrishna!!!!!

The regular Boyapati template is easy to recognise: an emotional family, a powerful hero, a cruel villain, high-voltage dialogues, top-class fights… and very weak physics.

But with Ram Charan and a big budget on board, Boyapati appears to have decided that normal excess was simply not enough.

So we get an OVER-emotional family, an OVER-powerful hero, an OVER-cruel villain, OVER-voltage dialogues and completely over-the-top fights.

And somehow the physics becomes even weaker than usual 😄

This time, the film does not stop with physics either.

Biology, geography and basic common sense all appear to receive similar treatment.

While Boyapati is busy pushing those limits, DSP’s music and BGM also disappointed me badly.

The one clear positive in the entire movie is Ram Charan.

He looks completely at ease delivering the high-voltage dialogues and throwing himself into the oversized fight sequences.

His commitment is never the problem.

The material surrounding him is.

For me, the movie becomes so exaggerated that even the usual suspension of disbelief expected from a Boyapati mass entertainer is not enough.

P.S. My daughter LOVED the movie!!!!! 😄

e: Petta is not trying to win anyone with airtight logic or a fresh story; it is designed to celebrate Rajinikanth’s screen presence after a run of slower, message-heavy films. Karthik Subbaraj understands that brief, Anirudh gives the mass moments a superb canvas, and Vijay Sethupathi, Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Simran add extra flavour.
v: Go get RAJINIfied!!! Karthik Subbaraj finally gives the Superstar a much-needed commercial potboiler, with Rajini’s style and Anirudh’s terrific BGM doing exactly what fans came for.
body:
Go get RAJINIfied!!!

After the social-message-oriented, slower films Rajinikanth had been doing with Pa. Ranjith, Karthik Subbaraj finally delivers the kind of commercial potboiler the Superstar badly needed 🙏

And because this is unapologetically a commercial Rajini movie, I am not going to spend much time worrying about logic or the basic storyline.

The real job here is to glorify Rajini’s screen presence and style — and Karthik does that successfully.

Anirudh’s BGM is terrific as usual and creates the perfect canvas for Rajini to unleash that seemingly never-ending stylish charisma.

The film also slips in a few cheeky political digs along the way, which I enjoyed 😛

Vijay Sethupathi and Nawazuddin Siddiqui do not get the meatiest roles of their careers, but both still become icing on the cake simply because of the quality they bring to the screen.

And after a long gap, it was genuinely pleasant to see Simran back on the big screen.

She looks beautiful, and the little romantic portions between her and Rajini are handled very sweetly.

Rajini’s very first dialogue carries the line, “Ayipoyanu anukunaru kadharaaaaaaa…” followed by that trademark laugh.

It almost feels intentionally written for the star himself.

His career may have gone through a low phase, but Petta is a reminder that he is never completely out of the race!!!!!

e: NTR: Kathanayakudu works best for viewers who simply want to relive NTR’s charisma and revisit famous incidents from his film career. For me, the lack of dramatic setbacks, the endless recreations and the difficulty of accepting Balakrishna as a much younger NTR make the three-hour film feel shallow despite his enormous effort and a few excellent scenes.
v: DISAPPOINTED!!! This material needed the breathing room of a multi-season web series, not a three-hour parade of familiar movie moments. Balayya gives 1000%, but the film lacks depth for a wider audience.
body:
DISAPPOINTED!!!

I honestly think this story could have worked much better as a multi-season web series rather than a single movie.

When I watch a biopic, I broadly see three kinds of audiences.

One group wants to relive the charisma of the person.

Another wants to understand the ups and downs of that life and how the person overcame challenges.

And a third group does not care about either — they simply want a good movie.

Mahanati became such a classic for me because it had enough content to satisfy all three groups.

NTR: Kathanayakudu struggles badly with that balance.

After NTR’s initial period of struggle, there are simply not enough failures or major dramatic conflicts in this portion of his life to sustain three hours of cinema.

There are four or five scenes that genuinely elevate the drama, but that is too little to carry such a long film.

There is also the obvious challenge of Balakrishna playing his own father across different ages.

It is relatively easy to make a younger actor look older with makeup.

Doing the reverse is much harder.

For me, it was difficult to accept Balayya as a young man beginning his journey and chasing his dreams.

That said, Balakrishna puts in 1000% effort to make the film memorable for his family, party and hardcore NTR fans.

The problem is not the commitment; it is that the movie itself never develops enough depth to reach a much larger audience.

The Mayabazar/Lord Krishna recreation is excellently shot.

On the other hand, the self-congratulatory moments around Balayya himself could easily have been avoided.

The later part of the second half finally becomes engaging, but by then I was already exhausted by the endless movie recreations 😦

Watch it mainly for Balayya and for a high-level visual recap of stories and incidents many of us already know.

I only hoped the next part, Mahanayakudu, would offer more drama for all three kinds of audiences.

e: 2.0 worked for me as a focused futuristic sci-fi film rather than a regular star vehicle. Shankar builds the entire movie around one unusual idea, keeps commercial distractions to a minimum and pushes Indian visual effects towards an ambitious scale, while A.R. Rahman’s BGM and the final Rajini-heavy stretch deliver the spectacle.
v: Give 2.0 its due credit! Shankar’s out-of-the-box sci-fi concept, top-notch visualisation and world-class Rahman BGM prove why Indian cinema needs creators willing to dream this BIG.
body:
I had seen plenty of posts either celebrating or mocking 2.0’s collections, but for me the larger point was much simpler.

If a film this ambitious fails purely because audiences refuse to support the experiment, Indian cinema risks losing creators with the imagination of Shankar.

How on earth does this man keep coming up with such out-of-the-box concepts and visual ideas? 🙏

Like a big Hollywood genre film, 2.0 revolves around one central concept and avoids stuffing the screenplay with unnecessary commercial distractions.

Shankar’s visualisation is top-notch.

The scale of what he imagines also makes the CGI team’s job incredibly difficult, and throughout the movie you can sense the challenge of turning those drawings and ideas into convincing imagery.

Story-wise, one aspect I particularly loved is the decision to look at the human race itself from a negative angle.

After Avatar, I had rarely seen a mainstream spectacle take that kind of position so directly.

A.R. Rahman’s BGM is world class.

Rajini fans need to wait until roughly the final thirty minutes to get the full blast of trademark Superstar style, but when that stretch arrives the film knows exactly how to use him.

I can only wonder what Shankar might have achieved if the visual-effects process had been smoother and given him every tool he originally imagined.

And I do not think comparing this film mechanically with Baahubali makes much sense.

Baahubali is a grand period drama built on a familiar revenge foundation and packaged brilliantly by Rajamouli.

2.0 is a futuristic science-fiction film attempting a completely different kind of story and technical challenge.

Both deserve to be judged for what they are trying to achieve.

Shankar has repeatedly shown that he wants to build films around unusual ideas — whether it is I or this story about our dependence on mobile technology turning against humanity.

Give that creative ambition its due credit.

e: Deva Das has an ordinary plot and equally basic execution, but its casting changes the experience considerably. Nani’s effortless expressions and Nagarjuna’s screen presence give the film most of its charm, while an impressive BGM and regular laughs make it an easy time-pass watch if you leave the logical brain at home.
v: Neither great nor bad — just a good time-pass movie. Nani handles the acting, Nag handles the glamour 😄 and their chemistry rescues a very basic story and execution.
body:
Deva Das has a normal, basic storyline and equally basic execution.

You never feel as though you are watching a great movie, but you do not really feel as though you are watching a bad movie either.

The director tries to balance commercial entertainment with a message-oriented angle, and the biggest strength of that attempt is the casting.

The film understands how to use Nani’s natural acting ability and Nagarjuna’s superb screen presence, and that combination becomes the real game changer.

Coming to Nani… man, what an actor!!!!!

He makes everything look easy with those wonderfully natural and cute expressions 🙏

And then there is Nag.

His screen presence alone is enough in many scenes, and his fitness and handsome levels are outstanding.

It almost feels as though while Nani was busy handling the acting department, Nagarjuna took responsibility for the movie’s glamour department 😄

The heroines unfortunately do not get much to work with.

The songs are again average — almost every number sits in that neither-good-nor-bad zone.

The BGM, however, is quite impressive and gives the movie more energy than the soundtrack.

Overall, it is a good time-pass movie with regular laughs every few minutes, provided you are willing to keep the logical part of your brain comfortably at home.

e: C/o Kancharapalem may share a broad emotional space with films like Naa Autograph, but its execution and sensitivity put it well above most comparisons for me. The local setting, first-time actors, natural dialogue and small situational songs create an experience that feels lived-in rather than manufactured — a classic for viewers open to this kind of cinema.
v: What a movie!!! Familiar love-story territory becomes something far more sensitive and natural through rooted characters, unforgettable dialogues and beautifully meaningful little songs. Repeated-watch list for sure.
body:
First, thanks to Srikanth Dontharaju for inspiring — or forcing 😄 — me to watch this movie in a theatre.

Coming to the film itself… what a movie!!!!!

The broad idea may sit in a familiar emotional space alongside films like Naa Autograph and several other stories about love across different phases of life.

But in terms of execution and sensitivity, C/o Kancharapalem is well above most of them for me.

The vintage, rooted neighbourhood backdrop and the wonderfully natural dialogues create an impact that stays with you.

Even a simple exchange can carry enormous emotional weight because the film never feels as though it is trying to manufacture a “cinematic” line.

There are several such scenes and conversations throughout the movie — little moments that become powerful precisely because the characters feel like ordinary people rather than carefully designed film personalities.

The fact that so many of the actors were facing the camera for the first time actually adds to that natural quality.

You are not watching familiar stars performing ordinary people; you feel as though you are watching people from that world simply living their lives.

The short situational songs are another major strength.

They are simple, meaningful and blend beautifully into the atmosphere rather than arriving as commercial interruptions.

This will definitely be on my repeated-watch list once it is available to stream 🙂

P.S. This classic is not really designed for the regular commercial-movie crowd. If this is not your genre, please do not force yourself through it and then kill the soul of the film with expectations it never promised to satisfy 😄

e: Sanju openly presents itself as Sanjay Dutt’s version of events, so I did not see the positive framing as something the film was hiding. By focusing mainly on addiction and the TADA case, Rajkumar Hirani finds enough material to explore the complicated father-son relationship, deep friendship and his familiar criticism of TRP-driven media, backed by an excellent cast.
v: Hirani turns Sanju’s own version of the drugs and TADA years into a strong father-son and friendship drama. Ranbir becomes 200% Sanjay Dutt in performance, while Vicky refuses to be overshadowed.
body:
A lot of people criticised Sanju for showing Sanjay Dutt in a positive light and presenting him as though he were largely a victim.

My first thought was that those viewers may have missed the movie’s very opening setup, which makes it clear that this is Sanju’s version of the incidents.

Coming to the film itself, the plot concentrates mainly on two major chapters — his drug addiction and the TADA case.

That turns out to be enough for Rajkumar Hirani to build strong emotion around the relationship between a superstar father and his spoiled, troubled son, while also exploring the depth of a close friendship.

And in typical Hirani style, he also gives us his take on media houses forever running behind BREAKING NEWS.

The casting is excellent.

Vicky Kaushal, playing Sanju’s best friend, gives such a strong performance that he forces the audience to notice him even while sharing a film with Ranbir Kapoor, Paresh Rawal and Manisha Koirala.

Makeup-wise, Ranbir may resemble about 80% of Sanjay Dutt at various points.

Acting-wise, he becomes 200% Sanjay — especially in the Khalnayak-era portions and during the drug-addiction and rehabilitation sequences 🙏

He completely commits to the mannerisms without allowing the performance to become only mimicry.

The icing on the cake is Sanjay Dutt’s own cameo in the rolling-title song, which doubles down on the film’s criticism of TRP-hungry media.

My very personal disappointment? There was no mention of RGV or Daud — the first movie released after Dutt came out of jail following his first term 😛

That aside, Sanju works very well as the emotional version of the story Hirani chooses to tell.

e: Kaala doubles down on Pa. Ranjith’s preferred style even though that approach had already frustrated me in Kabali. The film rarely feels like a Rajinikanth vehicle, the exaggerated supporting characterisations and recurring rap interventions became exhausting, and even Nana Patekar is given a generic role — for me, Kabali was considerably better.
v: The good news: Pa. Ranjith did not change his storytelling after Kabali. The bad news: exactly the same thing 😄 Apart from a couple of Rajini moments, this tested my patience badly.
body:
The GOOD thing is that Pa. Ranjith did not change his style of storytelling after Kabali.

And the WORST thing is… Pa. Ranjith did not change his style of storytelling after Kabali!!!!! 😄

Rajinikanth may have accepted Kaala because the story and its social angle could help him connect strongly with the masses, particularly at a time when he was considering a political future.

But as a movie fan, I felt that decision came at the cost of torturing a large section of his film audience.

Apart from perhaps two scenes, this barely felt like a Rajini movie to me.

Many earlier Rajinikanth films carried strong social messages while still wrapping them inside commercial elements that made terrific use of his screen presence.

Here, Pa. Ranjith seems far more concerned with his own storytelling style and a collection of exaggerated characterisations that repeatedly tested my patience.

Special mention has to go to the RAP gang that appears to stay beside Kaala irrespective of the situation and rap its way through everything.

Even moments that should carry grief or tension are interrupted by these performances, and after a point I was simply exhausted by the creative choice 🙏

Nana Patekar is wasted in a fairly generic role, although he is such a strong performer that he still makes his presence felt whenever he appears.

Ultimately, if I have to compare the experience with Pa. Ranjith’s previous Rajini film, Kabali was far better than Kaala for me.

e: Officer is deliberately far removed from conventional star cinema: Nagarjuna’s cop runs when survival demands it, there is no standard heroine track or hero-elevation package, the violence is harsh and RGV’s odd camera angles remain unapologetically his own. Those choices will alienate many viewers, but I liked the focused two-hour conflict, intelligent action design, BGM and several sharp dialogues.
v: Go in with an open mind and Officer has plenty to like: a focused cop-vs-corrupt-cop story, realistic action, superb BGM and an RGV visual style that refuses normal commercial hero rules.
body:
Before talking about Officer itself, I think part of the disastrous word of mouth around it had very little to do with the actual film.

RGV’s recent off-screen attitude had rubbed many people the wrong way, and a section of the audience — including some reviewers — seemed determined to declare the movie a disaster even before release.

The second problem is that the film is intentionally realistic in ways that clash with regular hero expectations.

When Nagarjuna’s cop is in danger, he actually runs for his life and waits for the right opportunity instead of magically fighting five hundred goons.

The violence is also genuinely harsh in places, which makes the movie unsuitable for sensitive or family audiences.

And, of course, RGV continues using those strange camera angles that can be uncomfortable for viewers accustomed to conventional framing.

Now to the common complaint that the film has “no story.”

Were those people sleeping in the theatre? 😄

The film is only about two hours long and focuses on the conflict between a police officer who is secretly operating as a mafia leader and another officer who becomes falsely framed as part of that criminal world.

How much more plot does a focused two-hour action film really need?

Yes, Officer stays far away from typical commercial ingredients.

There is no conventional heroine track, no giant hero-elevation scenes and no endless punch-dialogue package.

Instead, the protagonist behaves like an actual vulnerable human being, and the female lead even fires more bullets than the hero in places 🙏

The movie still contains several thought-provoking lines about power, truth, enemies and the good and evil inside every person.

I do agree that RGV should eventually move beyond his endless fascination with underworld and mafia stories.

But for this film, he and Nagarjuna had repeatedly promised realistic, intelligent action and strong sound design — and they deliver that.

The BGM is excellent, while the beach sequence, Essel World episode and climax contain some of the better action staging in the movie.

I may have connected with Officer partly because I am an ardent RGV fan and his visual style has even influenced the way I take photographs.

But my wife and daughter liked the film as well.

So I would simply say this: go with an open mind and there is a fair chance you may enjoy it too.
