e: Mahanati succeeds with every kind of viewer I could imagine: people who lived through Savitri’s aura, later generations who knew the legend from family and films, and complete newcomers simply looking for a cinematic experience. Nag Ashwin’s narrative, the period craft, Samantha’s climax and astonishing lead performances make it a wonderful, deeply emotional experience.
v: An EPIC that works whether you grew up worshipping Savitri or barely knew her name. Nag Ashwin pulls you into the black-and-white era, Keerthy and Dulquer LIVE their roles, and three hours disappear in a heart full of emotion.
body:
To start with, I think the audience for Mahanati can roughly be divided into three groups.

The first is the older generation who actually lived through Savitri’s aura and want to see how today’s filmmakers have recreated that legend on screen.

The second is a slightly younger generation who may not have experienced her peak first-hand but still grew up knowing who Savitri was — a little like today’s kids knowing Chiranjeevi even if they did not witness his earliest years.

And then there is the third group: people who may have absolutely no idea who Savitri was and are not emotionally invested in her legacy at all. They simply entered the theatre for a cinematic experience.

The beauty of this EPIC is that all three groups can get glued to the film within the first twenty minutes and leave the auditorium with a heart full of emotions!!!!!

The first two groups will probably see it as a great tribute to a legendary actress.

The third group can enjoy it almost like a film-industry rise-and-fall drama in the emotional space of something like Madhur Bhandarkar’s Fashion, only surrounded by the gorgeous aura of 1950s and 1960s cinema.

Irrespective of your perspective, the film keeps you involved right through the rolling titles, and its long runtime never really feels long.

The director, cinematographer, dialogue writer and BGM composer make sure the audience gets lost in the beauty of that black-and-white era 🙏

Rather than narrating Savitri’s biography in a simple straight line, Nag Ashwin cleverly mixes it with the journey of a journalist, and that structural choice adds another layer to the film.

The opening itself gives you an idea of what kind of experience is coming.

And the climax — with superb dialogues and Samantha’s performance — is an absolute standout 🙏🙏🙏

Keerthy Suresh and Dulquer Salmaan do not merely play Savitri and Gemini Ganesan; they LIVE those characters.

Haa… I could keep writing about this movie, but I still would not be able to put 100% of the emotions I went through while watching it into words.

Thanks, Nag Ashwin, for the wonderful experience.

You dreamt about this biopic and made it big… VERY, VERY BIG!!!

e: 102 Not Out proves that strong writing and execution can do wonders without a huge canvas. Amitabh Bachchan and Rishi Kapoor are effortless, but the real stars are Umesh Shukla and writer Saumya Joshi, who turn a potentially heart-wrenching three-character story into a warm, funny and emotionally lasting experience.
v: A father wanting to send his son to an old-age home — when did we last get a premise this wonderfully strange and meaningful? Instead of a tear-fest, Amitabh and Rishi give us 100 minutes of genuine laughs with emotion quietly running underneath.
body:
Amitabh Bachchan and Rishi Kapoor are at that stage of their careers where they can choose scripts because the subject emotionally moves them or simply interests them — without worrying too much about so-called fan expectations or box-office formulas.

And here they have picked a subject that leaves a genuine emotional impact on the audience.

The script never really has to challenge the acting abilities of these two legends.

At this point, performances like these almost look effortless for them.

But it is the content and execution that keep you glued to the screen.

Come on… when was the last time we came across a story even half as unusual and meaningful as a father wanting to send his own son to an old-age home? 🙏

Given that premise, you might expect a heart-wrenching emotional ride packed with tears.

Instead, what we get is roughly one hour and forty minutes of genuine laughs with a constant undercurrent of emotion and message.

That balance is what I loved.

The story essentially revolves around only three major characters, and these are exactly the kinds of films that make you curious about the people behind the writing and direction rather than merely the star cast.

So full credit to director Umesh Shukla and writer Saumya Joshi.

Kudos to both of you for reminding us that superb content with a modest budget can still do wonders!!!!!

e: Bharath Ane Nenu did not win me over through originality; I felt Koratala Siva was drawing heavily from the political climate and films such as Leader. But he packages those familiar ideas extremely well, blending commercial hero elevations into the story, giving Mahesh Babu one of his strongest recent vehicles and tapping directly into audience frustration with politics and TRP-driven media.
v: A commercialised BLOCKBUSTER version of Leader! I may question how fresh Koratala’s core idea is, but once he layers in Mahesh’s intensity, terrific dialogues, DSP and perfectly placed elevations, the formula works effortlessly.
body:
To start with, I have never been a huge fan of Koratala Siva’s core story ideas.

I often feel he observes what is happening around him, finds a socially relevant idea and then fills it with commercial ingredients.

With Srimanthudu, for example, I personally saw echoes of the village-adoption conversations happening around schemes such as Sansad Adarsh Gram Yojana.

With Janatha Garage, the environmental angle reminded me of initiatives such as Haritha Haram, while parts of the hero-versus-system setup felt familiar from older RGV-style formulas.

Now coming to Bharath Ane Nenu…

My feeling — and this is only my point of view 😄 — is that Koratala looked at the political environment around us, watched something in the space of Leader, and bingo… the broad story foundation was ready.

But once that foundation is in place, he focuses completely on what he does very well: commercial packaging and hero elevation.

The elevation templates may remind you of Srimanthudu and Janatha Garage, yet they blend into this story effortlessly.

And there we go… a BLOCKBUSTER is ready!!!!!

This was obviously the best Mahesh Babu movie I had seen in quite some time.

The audience also connects instantly because so many of us were already vexed with the real political environment and with media houses forever chasing TRPs.

The film has some of the best dialogues I had heard in recent Telugu cinema.

Mahesh is intense as usual, and DSP’s music once again gives the material exactly the kind of commercial energy it needs.

In one sentence: Bharath Ane Nenu is a commercialised, BLOCKBUSTER version of Leader!!!!!

e: Rangasthalam is less about Sukumar showing off clever narrative tricks and more about performances and world-building. The long runtime may test some viewers, but the cast is excellent, the 1980s Godavari village is beautifully realised, DSP’s BGM and meaningful songs add enormous flavour, and Ram Charan finally gets to show the actor inside the star.
v: It may disappoint viewers expecting Sukumar’s usual intellectual games or anyone allergic to a three-hour runtime — but watch it for Charan, Samantha, Aadhi, Jagapathi Babu, Naresh and that gorgeous 1980s Godavari world, and there is plenty to LOVE.
body:
Rangasthalam may disappoint you if you are a huge fan of Sukumar’s more overtly intelligent, puzzle-like direction.

And it may definitely disappoint you if you are too impatient to sit through a movie whose runtime is close to three hours.

On the other hand, you can love this movie to the core if you watch it for the performances.

Ram Charan, Samantha, Aadhi, Jagapathi Babu and Naresh are all EXCELLENT.

You can also love the film simply for the excellent recreation of a 1980s Godavari village.

The world feels lived-in, textured and completely different from the polished commercial settings we usually get.

DSP’s BGM is terrific as usual, while the songs come with meaningful lyrics that genuinely add value to the atmosphere and characters.

Special shout-out to “Aa Gattununtava”, which has excellent lyrics but somehow did not become as dominant as the other chartbusters.

And finally, after almost a decade in films, Ram Charan really shows the audience what he can do as an actor.

This is the kind of performance that should make the ACTOR Chiranjeevi — not merely the Megastar or one of Telugu cinema’s greatest dancers — feel proud 🙏

I only hope Charan continues choosing scripts that give him this kind of opportunity.

e: Needi Naadi Oke Katha stays admirably raw and focused instead of adding commercial distractions. That same honesty may limit its reach with viewers looking only for easy entertainment, but average and below-average students can connect instantly with its pressures, its idea of what it means to ‘settle’ in life and Sree Vishnu’s wonderfully natural performance.
v: Somewhere between a VERY GOOD movie and a GREAT one. Raw, honest and instantly relatable for anyone who was never the class topper — though that refusal to add commercial sugar may keep the regular time-pass crowd away.
body:
Somewhere between a VERY GOOD movie and a GREAT movie!!!!!

Kudos to the director for keeping Needi Naadi Oke Katha raw, focused and completely to the point without forcing commercial ingredients into it.

Ironically, that is also what may prevent the movie from connecting with a section of the regular audience that enters a theatre mainly for time-pass entertainment.

Story-wise, though, it feels absolutely apt.

Any average or below-average student who has grown up under constant pressure about marks, jobs and the need to ‘settle’ in life can connect with the film almost instantly.

One dialogue especially stayed with me: there was a time when getting a government job meant you were settled; later it became a bank job; now it has become a software job!!!!! 🙏

That one thought captures so much of the constantly changing definition of success around us.

And Sree Vishnu… such a natural performer 🙏

After watching him here, I made a mental note not to casually miss his films.

e: Tholiprema may have worked for almost everyone around me, including my friends and parents, but I remained completely disconnected from its romance. I liked several dialogues, the cinematography and the mature work from Varun Tej and Raashii Khanna; unfortunately the contrived romantic setup and familiar hero-heroine ego conflict overwhelmed those positives for me.
v: Hmmm… totally disconnected!!! Pretty visuals, mature performances and a few lovely dialogues cannot rescue a love story whose love-at-first-sight logic and familiar ego clashes simply do not work for me.
body:
Hmmm… I felt totally disconnected!!!!!

Maybe I first need to understand why I have become so resistant to pure love stories 😄

I was actually trying to remember the last full-fledged romance I genuinely loved — Love Aaj Kal? Cocktail? Anand? Godavari?

My bigger problem is that I keep waiting for our filmmakers to give us more realistic love stories instead of repeatedly falling back on love at first sight, convenient situations and the assumption that the heroine will eventually fall for the hero because he fights for her.

Some scenes here simply pushed that irritation further.

Who gets off a train these days to fetch drinking water from a tap? 🙏

And the hero-heroine ego conflict is something Telugu cinema has been revisiting since at least Kushi.

Having said all that, almost every friend of mine liked the movie — even my parents liked it.

So perhaps the only fair explanation is: thanks, RGV, for completely messing up my taste for love stories!!!!! 😄

P.S. When the entire Telugu audience was going gaga over Ye Maaya Chesave, I was probably one of the few people who hated that too 😦

I did love a few dialogues here, especially the thoughts about caste, remembering people’s mistakes more easily than their love, and how those who pretend to be angry with us can sometimes be the ones who love us most.

The cinematography and visuals are excellent, and Varun Tej and Raashii Khanna give mature performances.

Those positives are real — the romance simply did not connect with me.

e: AWE! is the kind of unusual film that can divide viewers completely, yet its ambition kept surprising me throughout. Regina Cassandra delivers the standout performance, the BGM is terrific, the humour often carries a thoughtful edge and even the lone song neatly reflects the film’s central conflict.
v: You may leave thinking it was AWEsomely AW(E)ful or AW(E)fully AWEsome — but every few minutes it gives you something to feel AWE about. Regina, the terrific BGM and witty, thoughtful dialogues stand out.
body:
After watching AWE!, you may come out feeling it was AWEsomely AW(E)ful or AW(E)fully AWEsome 😄

But one thing is almost guaranteed: every five or ten minutes, the film gives you something that makes you feel AWE!!!!!

The BGM is terrifically AWEsome and plays a huge role in holding together such an unusual collection of moods and characters.

There are many performers in the film, but Regina Cassandra’s terrific performance definitely stands out.

The dialogues are humorous and thought-provoking, especially the exchanges involving Nani, Priyadarshi and Ravi Teja, along with a couple of lovely lines from Nithya Menen.

There is only one major song, but the lyrics are excellent.

“Shatruvai dehame… manasutho thalapade” almost sums up the entire story in a single line 🙏

Whatever side of the awesome-versus-awful debate you finally land on, this is definitely not a movie that passes without making an impression.

e: Padmaavat left me wondering what inspired Sanjay Leela Bhansali to fight so hard to make this particular story. The film is visually grand in places and Ranveer Singh is terrific, while Ratan Singh’s death and the jauhar sequence show Bhansali at his strongest; unfortunately Shahid Kapoor and Deepika Padukone feel badly underused and the core story never held me.
v: All that struggle for what felt to me like a very thin story of two married men obsessed with one woman. Ranveer, a few grand low-light frames and Bhansali’s final stretch are the limited saving graces.
body:
I kept wondering what inspired Sanjay Leela Bhansali to take up this project against so many odds.

For me, underneath all that scale and controversy was a surprisingly thin story about two already-married men and their obsession with one woman.

Apart from a few beautifully composed low-light grand frames and Ranveer Singh’s terrific performance, I found very little in the film that held me.

Shahid Kapoor has enormous acting talent, yet here he often feels reduced to a single-expression supporting presence.

And Deepika Padukone — who has delivered good performances even in films I disliked badly — is given such a restrained character that she too often feels almost expressionless.

There are moments where Bhansali’s brilliance absolutely shows.

The sequence in which Ratan Singh dies while fighting Khilji is handled powerfully.

And the entire jauhar episode is staged with the visual and emotional command you expect from Bhansali 🙏

I only wish the rest of the movie had given me enough story and character engagement to match those few standout stretches.

e: Agnyaathavaasi frustrated me because even if the core story was familiar, the screenplay and direction still had every opportunity to make it work. A few trademark Trivikram lines survive, but weak staging drains their impact, while Pawan Kalyan’s deliberately eccentric performance is stretched so far that what might have been fun in one scene becomes exhausting across a full film.
v: Sharmaaaa… Varmaaaaa… manakenti ee KHARMA!!! An inspired story needed sharper screenplay and direction; instead even a few Trivikram-mark dialogues lose their value inside a film that turns PK’s quirks into complete overkill.
body:
If the story itself is already inspired or familiar, then at the very least the screenplay and direction have to carry the film.

That is exactly where Agnyaathavaasi collapsed for me.

There are still a few trademark Trivikram dialogues, but the direction is so weak around them that even those lines lose much of their value.

Pawan Kalyan has a certain exaggerated, quirky performance style that fans can enjoy enormously when used in the right scene.

But if you stretch the same behaviour across an entire movie, what is charming for a few minutes can become complete overkill.

In Trivikram style, if I have to summarise my reaction to the film:

“Sharmaaaa… Varmaaaaa… manakenti ee KHARMA!!!!!” 😄

P.S. There was an aunty sitting behind me who laughed and shouted loudly through practically every scene and irritated me throughout the film — maybe the Jabardasth effect? 😛

Then the movie ended and she herself declared that it had no head or tail and was terrible.

After surviving the movie, I first wanted to ask her why she had tortured the rest of us for the entire runtime 😄

e: Tubelight asks Salman Khan to carry an offbeat emotional story through innocence, childishness and vulnerability rather than star power. I respect his wholehearted effort, but Kabir Khan’s casting never convinced me: fans struggle to accept Bhai as a fragile ‘Tubelight,’ while neutral viewers struggle to forget Bhai long enough to believe the character.
v: Salman the BHAI can carry routine films on sheer screen presence; Tubelight needed Salman the ACTOR to disappear into Laxman. That casting mismatch exposes every script weakness instead of hiding it.
body:
Salman Khan the BHAI can earn hundreds of crores even with mediocre, routine subjects simply because his screen presence is powerful enough to carry films like Dabangg, Ready or Prem Ratan Dhan Payo.

But that does not automatically mean Salman Khan the ACTOR can make every offbeat script work when the entire movie depends on his acting fitting a very specific character.

Bajrangi Bhaijaan had a strong storyline packed with different emotions and did not rely only on Salman’s acting range.

His enormous screen presence simply elevated already-strong material into a blockbuster.

Tubelight is different.

The script depends heavily on Laxman’s innocence, emotional bonding and childishness.

And that is exactly where I felt Kabir Khan failed in casting Salman.

With such a massive star inside the role, the (tube)light gets thrown directly onto the script’s loopholes instead of keeping them in the dark 😄

Full respect to Salman for the wholehearted effort he puts into becoming Laxman.

But there are certain performances where the actor has to disappear so completely that you forget everything you already know about the star.

For me, Salman never quite reaches that point here.

Bottom line: fans may not accept BHAI being a Tubelight, and regular audiences may struggle to digest Tubelight being played by BHAI!!!!!

e: Sarkar 3 suffers mainly because both the genre and Subhash Nagre’s world have become deeply familiar. RGV does not reinvent the formula, so viewers expecting another landmark are bound to be disappointed; still, the film contains all the genre ingredients and felt to me like a filmmaker who had not reached home again, but had at least rediscovered the road back.
v: The Godfather formula is beaten to death and Sarkar 3 brings no new WOW factor — but taken without impossible RGV expectations, the philosophical lines, Nagre aura, weird angles and Govinda BGM still make a serviceable return to familiar territory.
body:
The biggest problem with the Godfather-style genre is that after a point the stories and characterisations become repetitive and predictable.

After the first Sarkar, so many filmmakers tried to exploit this kind of power-politics setup that the genre was practically beaten to death.

So when RGV himself returned to Sarkar, many of us naturally expected him to give the genre a completely new angle or definition.

Unfortunately, he does not.

And I think a lot of the negative reaction came from exactly that gap between the expectation attached to RGV and what the film actually delivers.

I would even argue that, taken exactly as it is, this same movie might have been received as a decent hit if RGV’s name had not carried such enormous expectations.

Sarkar 3 still contains practically every required ingredient: powerful and philosophical one-liners, sophisticated businessmen, corrupt politicians, slow camera movements, weird camera angles and our own Govinda… Govinda… Goooovinda!!!!!

RGV does directional justice to that familiar world.

But by the third film, we are already accustomed to Subhash Nagre’s black clothes, white beard, silent-killer stare and the Govinda BGM.

So the WOW factor we experienced when we first watched Sarkar is naturally missing.

For the previous few years, I felt RGV had lost much of his golden filmmaking touch from an audience perspective and had become far more visible through social-media controversies.

With Sarkar 3, I would not say he is completely back home.

But he has definitely found the road back.

P.S. After spending so many years experimenting with slow motion, camera angles and different kinds of cameras, I really hope RGV now uncovers something genuinely new in filmmaking and storytelling that can once again make both audiences and filmmakers go AWE!!!!!

e: Baahubali 2 doubles down on everything Rajamouli does best: emotional payoff, larger-than-life elevations and brilliantly staged action powered by M.M. Keeravani’s score. Anushka’s Devasena and Rana’s Bhallaladeva dominate the concluding chapter, while the story takes centre stage strongly enough to answer anyone who felt the first film’s spectacle overshadowed its narrative.
v: Rajamouli playing completely to his strengths — ELEVATIONS, EMOTIONS and Keeravani’s deadly BGM!!! Devasena and Bhallaladeva become the pillars, Rana is terrific, and even supporting characters get full-impact hero moments.
body:
Rajamouli plays completely to his strengths!!!!!

Those elevation scenes… those emotions… and then Keeravani’s deadly BGM on top of them 🙏🙏

The man even gives a supporting character like Subbaraju a couple of proper elevation shots and somehow creates full impact.

Anushka as Devasena and Rana as Bhallaladeva are the two pillars of this concluding part.

Rana is terrific, especially through his expressions.

There are moments around Baahubali’s death where the look on his face alone carries enormous weight 🙏🙏

After watching the first part, I expected Sivagami’s character to dominate the sequel.

Instead, Rajamouli makes Devasena even more powerful and almost tells Sivagami, “Papa, pakkaki velli aadukommaaa” 😄

I used to think only Sukumar could make even title cards feel creatively special, but Rajamouli proved me wrong here too.

Logic can obviously be kept aside during some of the fights, but the action is staged TERRIFICALLY.

And after RGV’s Shiva, one of the most memorable uses of a chain inside a fight sequence for me came again in this climax 🙂

Some people complained after the first film that graphics dominated the story.

Then the second film arrived with story and emotion dominating the graphics, and somehow a few people managed to complain about that too 😄

Meeru elli dubbing cinemalu chusukondi poyi!!!!!

e: Begum Jaan worked for me through sheer emotional force rather than conventional action. The rustic writing, excellent performances and powerful music create goosebumps without needing elaborate stunt sequences, while Vidya Balan dominates the centre and even Chunky Panday becomes genuinely frightening. Its boldness may limit the family audience, but the impact is undeniable.
v: You know you are watching a GREAT movie when even Chunky Panday gets a scary, meaty role! Bold emotions, rustic dialogues, top-notch BGM and terrific performances — and Vidya is every bit Bollywood’s BEGUM JAAN.
body:
You know you are watching a GREAT movie when even Chunky Panday gets a meaty role and turns genuinely scary as Kabir!!!!!

And what a superb movie this is — full of bold emotions, rustic dialogues, top-notch BGM and excellent acting from practically every artist 🙏

You do not need giant stunts or elaborate action episodes to create goosebumps.

Sometimes all it takes is a great dialogue delivered at the right moment and music that knows exactly when to hit.

Begum Jaan repeatedly proves that.

And man… if Kangana is called the Queen of Bollywood, then Vidya Balan is absolutely her BEGUM JAAN!!!!!

I am not sure how commercially successful a film with this kind of bold content can be, especially when the so-called family audience may stay away.

But irrespective of box office, this movie is going to leave an impact on the people who watch it.

P.S. I had not watched the original Bengali version, so I was judging this film completely on its own.

e: Mister left me wondering how Varun Tej agreed to the film and convinced that Srinu Vaitla had not escaped the formula he was expected to change. Characters and subplots keep arriving without purpose, the second half becomes exhausting and the climax itself seems to multiply — a sprawling commercial mess rather than a coherent entertainer.
v: Buy one movie ticket and somehow THREE movies come searching for you 😄 Srinu Vaitla’s multithreading obsession turns a 2h40m film into a 10-hour experience, complete with three climaxes and character-artist employment for everyone.
body:
The official tagline says something like: if we go searching for love, love will come searching for us.

For me, Mister needed a more accurate tagline: buy a ticket for one movie and somehow THREE movies will come searching for you!!!!! 😄

I genuinely could not understand how Varun Tej agreed to this script.

I went in hoping Srinu Vaitla might finally have changed his familiar formula.

I came out with the much stronger belief that manam chachinaa eeyana maaradu 😄

Half the time I could not understand why so many characters were entering, what they were supposed to do, or what Vaitla himself planned to make them do.

It almost feels like a giant employment scheme for Telugu character artists 🙏

The Krishnadevaraya-family stretch in the second half is especially exhausting.

A movie that runs around two hours and forty minutes somehow creates the feeling that you have been sitting there for ten hours.

And just when you start desperately waiting for the climax… you get THREE climaxes and fresh tears of blood 😄

I suspect Srinu Vaitla developed a childhood fascination with the Java multithreading concept and has been faithfully applying the same architecture to his screenplays movie after movie.

e: Katamarayudu felt like a storyline that belonged in the 2000s filmed with visual effects from the 1990s. Pawan Kalyan’s screen presence and Ajay’s expressions are almost the only positives I found, while the music, BGM, supporting material and exaggerated performance choices make the entire package feel surprisingly cheap for a star vehicle.
v: Keep expectations underground, ignore the story, close your eyes for Shruti and somehow close both eyes AND ears for the songs… then maybe 😄 PK is the only real saving grace in a film that feels cheaply assembled around him.
body:
If you have been watching all the out-of-the-box films arriving around this period, then Katamarayudu comes with a few viewing instructions 😄

Do not expect too much.

Do not think too deeply about the story.

Close your eyes whenever required… and when the songs arrive, somehow find a way to close your ears along with them.

If you can manage all that, perhaps the movie becomes easier to survive 😄

This feels like a storyline that should have been made in the 2000s with CG work that looks as though it came from the 1990s.

The only real saving grace is Power Star Pawan Kalyan, supported in places by Ajay’s expressions.

The most irritating parts for me are Anup Rubens’ music and BGM, amplified further by Shruti Haasan’s exaggerated performance.

Apart from the “Oka Rayudoooo” BGM bit, I found the music horrible.

At this rate, Anup may have to wait another ten years before somebody hands him another huge star-hero film 😄

My bigger frustration is that the makers seem to think putting PK in the centre is enough.

Then the story, supporting cast, music and even Shruti’s styling can apparently be bought cheaply from the local market 🙏

For a film built around such a massive star, that surrounding carelessness is impossible to ignore.

e: Badrinath Ki Dulhania starts from themes I found worthwhile and realistic, especially dowry and the expectations placed on women. Varun Dhawan does justice to the Jhansi tapori and Alia Bhatt is effortless, but the commercial packaging repeatedly weakens the material until the film sits awkwardly between social drama and mainstream entertainer without fully succeeding as either.
v: An excellent, still-relevant plot about dowry and women’s independence gets trapped inside confused commercial treatment. Neither a strong issue-driven film nor a satisfying entertainer — and seriously, shouldn’t this have been Vaidehi Ka Dulha? 😄
body:
I normally start by talking about the good points of a movie, but here I could not hold myself back from laughing at one irony.

The entire plot revolves around women’s empowerment and opposition to dowry.

Varun’s character gradually becomes a better man under the influence of Alia’s character.

So why exactly is the movie called Badrinath Ki Dulhania?

Vaidehi Ka Dulha would have been a far more appropriate title 😄

These may look like small things, but they also show how deeply male-dominated our industry remains even while using words such as “women empowerment” for preaching.

Way to go, Dharma Productions and KJo 🙏

The actual story deals with dowry and women’s independence.

Some viewers may say the theme or screenplay feels like something from the 1990s, but unfortunately these issues still exist in many Indian families.

So full credit to Varun Dhawan for choosing the subject.

He does justice to the good-hearted Jhansi tapori, while the role is almost a cakewalk for Alia — nothing here really challenges the full potential of that little dynamite.

My problem is that the plot is excellent but the completely commercial treatment becomes the spoilsport.

At the end, you neither feel you watched a great story-driven movie nor a proper commercial entertainer.

If you watch it for the realistic issue, the way the film treats it can feel frustrating.

If you watch it purely as commercial entertainment, the serious storyline starts feeling awkward inside that packaging.

It gets trapped between its two intentions.

e: Nenu Local is one of those films where taking your logical brain into the theatre is actively dangerous. The story and screenplay make little sense, but Trinadha Rao Nakkina designs the hero for maximum entertainment and Nani gives that character 200%, while DSP gets room to try a few different musical ideas. As entertainment, it works almost entirely because of Nani, Nani and Nani.
v: Forget ‘Attitude is Everything’ — here NANi’s attitude is everything! Logic must be switched off at the theatre door, but Nani’s effortless performance turns a completely illogical story into pure paisa-vasool entertainment.
body:
The tagline says “Attitude is Everything”, but for this movie a more accurate version would be: “Nani’s attitude is the ONLY thing!!!!!”

How does this man act with such ease? 🙏

I may be exaggerating, but watching him here genuinely made me feel he could become one of the next really big things in Telugu cinema.

Not working with a massive star also seems to free DSP a little, and he tries some different tunes instead of falling into the same patterns I had heard in several of his other films.

Just like Cinema Choopistha Mava, the director does what he knows best: take an illogical story, design a typical hero who can generate entertainment and then let the actor carry it.

Nani gives that character 200% justification.

Story and screenplay-wise, though, this is almost Sajid Khan territory 😄

You should not dare to take your logical brain into the theatre.

Along with the standard “switch off your mobile phone” warning, perhaps the makers should have added another notice asking viewers to switch off their brains too.

But purely as entertainment? PAISA VASOOL — because of Nani, Nani and Nani!!!!!

e: Appatlo Okadundevadu tracks the rise and fall of Railway Raju and Imtiaz almost like two destinies moving in opposite rhythms. The direction and editing are terrific, every scene feels relevant, contemporary ideas such as piracy and real-estate change are woven intelligently into the period story, and Sree Vishnu leads a uniformly strong cast in a rare film that stays entertaining without formula tracks.
v: Glad I did NOT miss this one. Railway Raju vs Imtiaz vs TIME itself — terrific direction, editing, screenplay and BGM, with not one irrelevant scene and no formula-comedy crutch needed to keep you hooked.
body:
Glad I did not miss this movie!!!!!

At its heart, Appatlo Okadundevadu is Railway Raju versus Imtiaz… but also both of them versus TIME and DESTINY.

The film wonderfully tracks the rise, fall, rise, fall and rise of Railway Raju’s fate against the fall, rise, fall and rise of Imtiaz.

The direction and editing are terrific.

I could hardly find a scene or shot that felt irrelevant to the story.

The way the writer-director connects things like the switch hit, piracy and Kukatpally real estate with changing times shows real intelligence.

The screenplay fits the story perfectly.

The BGM is terrific too, while the songs blend with the story even though the tunes themselves could have been stronger.

This is one of those rare films that proves you do not need formula ingredients or a separate comedy track to keep an audience hooked and entertained.

The performances are excellent across the board — Sree Vishnu, Nara Rohit, Prabhas Sreenu, Brahmaji, Rajeev Kanakala and Ajay all contribute strongly.

Sree Vishnu once again proves what a wonderful actor he is.

I kept wondering how Telugu cinema had managed to underuse someone this natural for so long.

And take a bow, Rohit, for returning to your experimentation zone and also backing the film as a producer 🙏

e: Shatamanam Bhavati takes an age-old family-and-village template and shows that execution can still make familiar material feel fresh. Beautiful visuals and characters who resemble people we actually know keep the film warm and engaging, even if the songs and BGM could have been stronger. For me, it was simply a perfect family entertainer.
v: A perfect family entertainer — LOVED IT TO THE CORE. The story is a kichidi of familiar village-family films, but clean entertainment, lovely visuals and recognisable people prove that freshness does not always require a new plot.
body:
A perfect family entertainer — LOVED IT TO THE CORE!!!!!

You do not always need an exceptional, out-of-the-box story or complicated screenplay to keep an audience engaged.

Sometimes you can create magic with an age-old story simply by giving it clean, fresh entertainment.

Story-wise, Shatamanam Bhavati is almost a kichidi of many familiar family films and village-backdrop movies.

But the beautifully captured visuals and the entertainment coming from characters who feel surprisingly real are what keep the movie engaging.

Apart from the central characters played by Prakash Raj, Anupama and Sharwanand, many of the people around them feel like relatives or neighbours you could actually recognise from your own life.

That familiarity works in the film’s favour rather than against it.

The songs and BGM could definitely have been better.

But as a warm family watch, the movie gave me exactly what I wanted.

e: Khaidi No. 150 did not need an original story to work for me because I was there for Chiranjeevi’s comeback, and he delivers exactly the reminder fans wanted. His comedy timing, emotional ease, drunk performance, graceful dancing and sheer screen presence dominate everything around him. There may be little else to discuss — but Boss okkadu chaalu 😄
v: Did I go for a fresh story? NO — this was the BOSS comeback movie! Comedy timing, drunk act, emotion, graceful dance and pure screen fire… BOX-OFFICE AMMA MOGUDU IS BACK WITH A BANG!!!!!
body:
How exactly did Tamil audiences see this as some extraordinary story? 😄

Telugu cinema alone could probably show you another 150 films built around broadly similar ideas.

But wait a minute… did I enter Khaidi No. 150 looking for a different story or radical execution?

NO!!!!!

This was the BOSS COMEBACK MOVIE.

And yes — the Boss with that kick-ass comedy timing is BACK.

The Boss who can play a drunkard with perfect ease is BACK.

The Boss who is terrific in emotional scenes is BACK.

The Boss who can set the silver screen on fire with those graceful dance steps is BACK.

And YES… THE BOX-OFFICE AMMA MOGUDU IS BACK WITH A BANG!!!!!

My four-year-old daughter was dancing inside the theatre during the songs, and that alone felt like the perfect reminder that one of Telugu cinema’s biggest entertainers had returned.

Honestly, apart from Boss there is not much I feel like discussing about the movie.

But then again… Boss okkadu chaalu 😛

e: Gautamiputra Satakarni worked for me as a solid period film rather than the oversized cultural event surrounding its release. Krish and Balakrishna put in their best effort, the dialogues are excellent and the direction is focused; considering the budget, schedule and the physical demands on its lead, the result is genuinely impressive even if I would stop short of calling it essential viewing.
v: Not a must-watch or some mystical ‘Telugu pride’ event — just a GOOD historical film made with impressive limitations. Krish directs sharply, the dialogues roar, and honestly no one fits Satakarni better than Balayya.
body:
A good movie with some of the best effort from Krish and Balakrishna.

And yes — I honestly do not think anyone else could have suited the role better than Balayya Babu.

I would not call Gautamiputra Satakarni a MUST WATCH, but it is definitely a good watch.

My only advice is not to enter carrying all the giant hype around Telugu jaathi gouravam and similar slogans.

At the end of the day, treat it as a normal historical period film and judge what is actually on the screen.

From that perspective, there is plenty to appreciate.

The dialogues are excellent, Krish’s direction is precise and who else do we really have who can mouth those giant, thunderous lines with quite the same conviction as Balakrishna? 😄

Also, the scale needs to be viewed in context.

Considering the limitations of budget and production time — along with Balayya’s age and the physical demands of the role — the team has delivered a fantastic effort.

So ignore the cultural-event baggage, watch it simply as cinema, and there is a solid historical entertainer here.

e: Dangal is superbly made cinema, with exceptional casting and visible commitment from every performer and technician. My major reservation is not the filmmaking but the real-life framing: I could not fully celebrate a story that seemed to glorify Mahavir Phogat’s methods more than the daughters who sacrificed so much to fulfil his ambition.
v: As a FILM, I loved it to the core — pitch-perfect casting and 300% effort everywhere. As a real-life story, though, I hated the way a father forcing his dream onto his daughters gets turned into unquestioned heroism.
body:
As a FILM, I absolutely loved Dangal to the core.

Every artist and technician seems to have put in 300%, and that effort is visible on the silver screen.

The casting is pitch perfect.

But the moment I think about it as a real-life story, my reaction becomes much more complicated.

I actually hated one major aspect of the way the story is framed.

Rather than primarily glorifying the Phogat sisters — who sacrificed so much of their childhood and personal freedom to fulfil their father’s dream — I felt the film spends too much energy glorifying the father who imposed that dream on them with very little mercy.

I fully understand that Mahavir Phogat’s ambition was to win a medal for the nation.

But does a noble destination automatically justify forcing your own unrealised dream onto your children?

Are we calling him a hero only because his daughters eventually succeeded and made the country proud?

What if those same girls had trained just as hard and failed?

Would the methods suddenly look very different?

By that logic, every parent who forces a child into engineering or medicine because it represents the parent’s definition of success should also be treated as a hero.

So I have two reactions living together here: excellent cinema that I loved watching, and a real-life interpretation that I strongly question.

That tension is exactly what keeps Dangal from becoming an uncomplicated five-star film for me.

e: Vangaveeti gave me the RGV craft I expected — haunting BGM, striking visuals, balanced dialogues and unconventional staging — but this time with a story strong enough to match it. What I especially liked is that the film avoids simple hero-villain labels and instead lets circumstance and miscommunication become the real destructive forces, capped by a final line that reminded me why I admire RGV’s storytelling instincts.
v: RGV films usually have awesome taking, camera, lights, BGM and acting… except sometimes the STORY. This time even the story is there 😄 Nobody handles morally grey political violence and makes situations the villain quite like him.
body:
Generally, in an RGV movie, the taking, camera work, lighting, BGM and acting can all be awesome… and then the story may be the one missing ingredient 😄

This time, even the STORY is there!!!!!

One thing I have always admired about RGV’s style is how he handles controversial real-life material.

He does not necessarily decide that one person must be the HERO and somebody else must be the VILLAIN.

Instead, he can make situations, ego, timing and miscommunication the real villains while leaving the human characters somewhere in the grey zone.

Very few filmmakers can do that as naturally as he can.

The BGM, as with many of his stronger films, has that haunting quality that stays with you.

The dialogues are also nicely balanced — impactful without constantly announcing which side the audience is supposed to support.

RGV even seems to take a sweet-and-hot little revenge on some of the people who created noise around preventing the film’s release 😛

You will understand what I mean once you watch it.

And finally… the entire movie is one thing, but the dialogue that arrives at the very end is another level altogether.

That one final touch simply reminded me again how sharp the master can be when his cinema and his instincts are fully aligned 🙂

e: Dear Zindagi turns a confused, emotionally messy young woman — the kind of person many of us know as a sibling, cousin, friend or colleague — into a warm and recognisable story. Shah Rukh Khan is wonderfully mature and generous, but Alia Bhatt disappears so completely into Kaira that she makes you laugh, pity her, get irritated with her and cry with her, all backed by excellent situational music.
v: What a movie… Gauri Shinde is bang on target! SRK gives his most mature, impactful work in years while creating space for Alia — except there is no Alia here, only KAIRA. Their combination is an absolute treat.
body:
What a movie… Gauri Shinde is bang on target!!!!!

If English Vinglish was about a housewife finding herself, Dear Zindagi is about a young woman struggling to understand her own choices and emotions.

And she is not some distant movie character.

She feels like somebody we have all encountered — a sibling, cousin, friend, colleague, girlfriend or simply someone in our everyday life who cannot quite figure out what decision to make next.

SRK: this year once again reminded me why he can still be the Badshah of acting in Bollywood.

After Fan, this is another superb performance.

I had not seen him this mature and quietly impactful for a long time — probably since films like Chak De! India and Swades.

What I loved even more is the space he creates for Alia to perform.

The SRK–Alia combination is an absolute treat to watch.

Aaaliaaaaa!!!!! The wonder kid of Bhatt saab 😄

After RGV, she may be one of the few film personalities I can happily argue with anyone about.

I actually went to the movie primarily to watch Alia.

But what shocked me was that after a point there was no Alia on screen — there was only KAIRA.

She makes you laugh at her, feel pity for her, get irritated by her and eventually cry with her.

For the first time in a long while, I felt SRK had to deliver an extraordinary performance simply to match the actor standing opposite him — something I had previously associated with his scenes alongside Amitabh.

And she was only 23, already carrying performances in Highway, Udta Punjab and now Dear Zindagi 🙏

The music is really good and genuinely situational, with especially lovely songs and lyrics.

On a completely selfish final note: I would still LOVE to see RGV and Alia work together someday 😄

e: Sahasam Swasaga Sagipo is a sharply divided experience for me: the romantic first hour was painful because that genre rarely works for me, while the later semi-action stretch suddenly becomes gripping. Naga Chaitanya gives what I felt was his best performance to that point, the BGM is superb and the much-criticised climax actually felt realistic to me.
v: A one-hour transformation from ‘What the F***’ to ‘WHAT A F***’ 😄 The romance nearly lost me, but once the film shifts gears it becomes a BANG, with Chaitanya’s best performance till then and a climax I actually loved.
body:
What an awesome transformation from “What the F***” to “WHAT A F***!!!!!” 😄

And no, the four-letter word does not stand for FILM 😛

The first hour was horrible for me.

That is partly personal because I am simply not a fan of the romance genre, and the early stretch leans heavily into exactly that zone.

But after that… BANG!!!!!

The movie suddenly shifts gears and becomes much more engaging.

I saw several reviews saying the climax was weak, but personally I loved it.

In fact, I thought the way it resolved the situation felt more realistic than the giant heroic ending many films would have chosen.

Undoubtedly, this was Naga Chaitanya’s best performance for me till that point.

Manjima Mohan fits the role well, and the supporting characters also feel appropriate rather than distracting.

The BGM is superb.

The music itself is okay — again, I am not the biggest fan of Rahman’s slower romantic songs — and I had my usual complaints about some of the lyrics.

The funny part is that Vellipomakey almost sounds like the film itself talking to the audience during that first hour: “Vellipomakandi… stay here, the movie is going to become superb after this” 😛

Overall, it is a good movie for viewers who enjoy a romance-to-action transition and can survive that opening stretch.

Whatever my genre bias, I did feel the central concept and story were grounded in realism right from the beginning.

e: I had not watched the Malayalam original, so I entered the Telugu Premam without comparison baggage. Naga Chaitanya delivers one of his better performances, Shruti Haasan is effortless, the music and visuals suit the story, and Praveen’s comedy becomes the crucial ingredient that keeps a romance-averse viewer like me happily involved.
v: I usually get bored by pure romance, yet Premam kept me engaged — largely because Praveen’s comedy keeps the emotions light. Think Naa Autograph minus the heavy sentiment, plus easy entertainment.
body:
I had not watched the original Malayalam version, so my reaction to Premam was not pre-programmed by comparisons.

Four people especially stood out to me.

Naga Chaitanya clearly tries his best and, for the most part, succeeds in giving one of his strongest performances till then.

He also looks stylish across the other stages of the character’s life.

Praveen, to be frank, carries a huge portion of the movie through his comedy timing and expressions.

That contribution was particularly important for me because pure romantic films usually start making me feel bored very quickly 😄

Srinivas plays an important role during the final half hour, while Shruti Haasan handles her character with complete ease.

The music and BGM are good and suit the plot nicely.

The visuals in the Evare song are especially delightful to watch.

The dialogues are also very good.

I particularly liked the thought that love, hatred and anger are all feelings — we may want those feelings to grow, but whether they remain can depend on the other person too.

To cut it short: love and romance movies have always had the power to bore me, but Premam keeps me engaged because it constantly balances the romance with entertainment.

Without the comedy I might have had a completely different reaction.

For me, it is almost Naa Autograph minus the heavy emotions plus light-hearted comedy.

e: ISM is unmistakably Puri Jagannadh, built around aggressive one-liners, attitude and a much tighter second half. Kalyan Ram looks completely at ease and gives especially strong work later in the film. I enjoyed the Puri flavour enough to recommend it to his audience, even while feeling increasingly that his writing would benefit from bringing other storytellers into the room.
v: Pure Puri markISM — his dialogue bombs have graduated into MISSILES 😄 The second half is racy, Kalyan Ram is uber-cool and excellent, and Puri fans should absolutely watch it… though it is time he borrowed someone else’s story once in a while.
body:
This is purely PURI markISM!!!!!

Movie after movie, Puri Jagannadh’s dialogue bombs seem to be upgrading themselves into MISSILES 😄

The language is unapologetically Puri — angry, provocative, funny and sometimes deliberately vulgar.

Whether he is talking about the farmer who grows everyone’s food, corruption by people who look exactly like us, attraction, or a stupid misunderstanding around the word “duck,” the lines arrive with that unmistakable Puri rhythm.

The second half is racy and to the point, and that is where the movie works best for me.

At the same time, I really do feel it is time for Puri to start taking stories from other writers occasionally.

His voice is still powerful, but the basic story foundations would benefit from somebody else bringing fresh material into that voice.

Kalyan Ram is uber-cool and delivers excellent acting, particularly in the second half.

He looks completely comfortable with the attitude and energy the film demands.

Bottom line: worth watching if you enjoy Puri-mark cinema.

Migitha vaallu Brahmotsavam ki velli manchi maatalu vinandi 😄

e: Mana Oori Ramayanam has a distinctive single-point premise and deliberately avoids loud dialogue or commercial decoration. Prakash Raj and Priyamani are predictably strong, while Prudhvi surprises with a serious, mature performance and Ilaiyaraaja’s music fits the restrained mood. Its slow, subtle approach will not connect with everyone, but the experiment deserves appreciation.
v: A different, mature concept carried by understated emotions and strong performances. It may feel much longer than its two hours to a regular audience, but lovers of unusual cinema should give it a one-time watch.
body:
A different story and concept with emotions running quietly underneath!!!!!

Prakash Raj and Priyamani nail their performances — which, frankly, is exactly what you expect from actors of their calibre.

The surprise for me is Prudhvi.

After years of seeing the “30 Years Industry” comedy image, watching him deliver a serious, mature performance adds another dimension to the film.

The movie is hardly two hours long, yet a normal audience may feel as though it is running for ages.

That is because the film stays focused on a single point and works through subtle emotion rather than heavy dialogues, comedy tracks or constant dramatic turns.

Ilaiyaraaja’s music is good and fits the material well without trying to overpower it.

Even though the movie received a clean U certificate, I can imagine many viewers not connecting with the mature and somewhat bold core concept.

So hats off to Prakash Raj for taking that kind of storyline and still moulding it into a clean film.

For regular commercial audiences, this may be a difficult sit.

For movie lovers who actively encourage different concepts, it is worth a one-time watch.

e: Majnu is deliberately ordinary: a routine romance built almost entirely on Nani’s charm, with a small but effective Raj Tarun cameo. It drags in places and viewers expecting another Nani wonder may be disappointed, but with modest expectations the clean comedy, easy music and much stronger final stretch make it a watchable time-pass film.
v: Simple story, simple screenplay, simple music, simple comedy — no WOW and thankfully no VAMMOO either 😄 A few drags, a strong final ten minutes and Nani carrying almost everything make it perfectly time-passable.
body:
A simple story with a simple screenplay, wrapped in simple music and simple comedy!!!!!

There is no big WOW factor anywhere in Majnu.

But thankfully there is no giant VAMMOO factor either 😄

The movie drags in a few places, but it remains watchable.

After a couple of months filled with either different-genre experiments or routine oorra-mass entertainers, this feels like somebody simply took a regular story and invested almost everything in Nani’s performance, with a small bonus investment in Raj Tarun’s cameo.

If you enter with no expectations, there is a fair chance you will like it.

If you go in expecting another extraordinary Nani film because of his recent form, you may come away disappointed.

The entire movie is one level… and the final ten minutes are another.

Going by the idea that all’s well that ends well, the stronger finish helps the overall experience considerably.

So yes — it is comfortably time-passable.

To conclude, Nani is the SOLE and SOLO of this film, with a small but effective assist from Raj Tarun.

e: PINK is an intense, morally clear film that needs no grand production scale because its real production value is conviction. Taapsee Pannu and the other women are terrific, Amitabh Bachchan is powerful, the writing is bold and the music stays perfectly aligned with the tension. It is not entertainment-first cinema; it is a message delivered exactly as forcefully as intended.
v: TERRIFIC movie, TERRIFIC performances and dialogues with HUGE impact. Taapsee completely dominated the screen for me — and the film’s plot, music and performances are BANG ON to one simple truth: NO means NO.
body:
TERRIFIC movie with TERRIFIC performances!!!!!

Taapsee Pannu and the other two lead women are superb, followed by Amitabh Bachchan.

In fact, from my perspective, Taapsee completely dominates even Amitabh in this film.

And it made me wonder again: how did Telugu cinema waste this woman’s talent for so long by mostly limiting her to glamorous roles? 😦

Story and dialogues: it takes guts and boldness to write an intense subject like this and then support it with lines that create HUGE impact.

Take a bow, everyone involved.

Music and BGM: completely apt and perfectly in sync with the movie’s intensity.

Production-value-wise, the film does not depend on giant locations or visual extravagance; much of it unfolds around a courtroom and a colony.

But if we are talking about MORAL values, that is a different conversation entirely.

Do NOT watch this movie if you are expecting conventional entertainment.

Do NOT watch it if you assume an independent working woman is automatically available for sex.

Do NOT watch it if you believe a woman wearing modern clothes, smoking or drinking means her character is questionable.

And finally… do NOT watch it if you cannot understand that NO means NO.

Because if you carry those attitudes into the theatre, you will probably hate the movie and then talk badly about it — which would be a disgrace to the effort the whole team has put in.

For me, the plot, dialogues, music and performances are absolutely BANG ON for what PINK wants to communicate.

e: Jyo Achyutananda pulled me in from its playful title cards and kept rewarding me with Srinivas Avasarala’s sharp screenplay and wonderfully witty dialogue. Nara Rohit owns an unusually practical character without demanding artificial justification, Naga Shaurya and Regina fit beautifully, and the emotional second half completes rather than weakens the comedy-heavy opening.
v: Sensible, neat, clean, witty, entertaining, emotional, engaging… the list goes on! Srinivas Avasarala turns a simple story into top-notch writing, with realistic characters, terrific performances and a second half I liked even MORE for letting emotion take over.
body:
Sensible. Neat. Clean. Witty. Entertaining. Emotional. Engaging… and the list goes on and on!!!!!

You are involved right from the beginning.

Even something as simple as the title cards, backed by 1990s super-hit songs, immediately shows the director’s sensibility.

Srinivas Avasarala — take a bow for your intelligence.

The story is simple, the first-half screenplay is top-notch and the dialogues are toooooooo good.

What I especially loved is the way silly lines and deliberately broken-English jokes are woven naturally into a clean family entertainer and still produce genuine laughs.

The characterisation is another major strength, especially Nara Rohit’s Achyuth.

The film never desperately tries to give some grand explanation or justification for his practical, emotionally detached attitude.

That lack of forced justification actually makes him feel more realistic.

And yes, I call parts of the story realistic because my brother and I once flirted with the same girl who lived in the apartment above ours when I was in fifth or sixth class 😄

I have been a fan of Nara Rohit’s film choices since Banam, so I was particularly happy to see him hit the bullseye here.

He owns Achyuth completely.

His performance is superb — although, as Rowdy Fellow already taught us, babu koncham boddu ga kaadhu… baaaagha laavu ayyadu 😄

Naga Shaurya is extremely good for a young actor; the innocence in his face and his work in the emotional portions stand out.

Regina fits Jyo perfectly, particularly the modern yet mature way the character is written.

Kalyan Ramana’s music is soothing, the BGM stays light and the title track is melodious.

The cinematography is also very good and exactly suited to the film.

I saw many reviews complaining about the second half becoming less funny.

Come on — you cannot expect every minute of a film to be a laugh riot.

The second half is the CORE of the movie, where emotion takes the front seat.

And for me, yes… it is very, very, VERY good.

e: Janatha Garage did not impress me with originality; I found Koratala Siva leaning heavily on a familiar RGV-style power-system template despite adding an environmental angle. But the performances transform the experience: Mohanlal and especially NTR are formidable, and DSP’s background score gives the second half the force the story itself lacks.
v: Koratala Siva’s version of RGV’s Sarkar — nothing really new in story or execution, but Mohanlal and NTR are POWER PACKED, NTR’s second-half work is excellent and DSP’s BGM haunted me enough to become ringtone material.
body:
To put it very simply, Janatha Garage is Koratala Siva’s version of RGV’s Sarkar!!!!!

Story-wise and execution-wise, I did not find much that felt genuinely new.

But the movie has POWER-PACKED performances from Mohanlal and NTR.

NTR… take a bow.

His expressions and dialogue delivery are simply EXCELLENT, especially through the entire second half.

Watching NTR movies had usually been a lower priority for me up to that point.

I watched Temper mainly for Puri, Nannaku Prematho for Sukumar and Janatha Garage for the combination.

After this performance, though, I made a decision to watch his next films for NTR himself.

I only hope he keeps experimenting irrespective of purely commercial outcomes.

DSP’s BGM was still haunting me after the movie.

My ringtone was definitely in danger of changing 😄

Now coming back to Koratala Siva… I did have one uncomfortable question: was this the beginning of a creative decline?

The basic power-and-justice story template felt like something RGV had already used, reused and almost exhausted.

Koratala adds the hero’s environmentalism, but even there I had to laugh at the fact that this great environmental lover still moves around on a bike instead of a cycle or at least public transport 😄

As for Kajal Aggarwal, Samantha and Nithya Menen — they do the jobs they are given.

For me, the film ultimately succeeds much more because of NTR, Mohanlal and DSP than because of anything particularly fresh in its story.

e: Kabali is not the nonstop Rajini-style mass film the gigantic pre-release expectations conditioned many viewers to expect. Going in with zero expectations, I found a good, deliberately slow family story inside a gangster setting, with Rajinikanth showing vulnerability and acting rather than relying only on trademark style, and Radhika Apte giving him formidable company.
v: Forget the impossible hype and watch what is actually there: a slow, emotional family drama inside a mafia backdrop, with Rajini finally getting room to ACT and Radhika Apte at times dominating even him.
body:
Maybe it was time for the Superstar to take a small break and let his confused audience decide exactly what kind of roles they wanted their ageing icon to play 😄

Thanks to all the negative buzz, I entered Kabali with zero expectations.

What I saw on screen was actually a beautiful family drama with emotions, placed against a mafia backdrop.

Yes, the movie is sloooooow.

But that kind of deliberate pace is hardly unusual in Tamil cinema.

More importantly, Rajini nails the acting — not through his regular style tricks, but by getting the rare opportunity to show vulnerability.

I genuinely had to think back and ask myself when we had last seen a Rajinikanth film give him this much space to perform, especially in scenes such as Kabali’s desperate search for his wife.

Special mention to Radhika Apte.

She is so strong that at times she completely dominates Rajini in sheer screen presence.

I also heard people blaming the PR team for creating unreasonable expectations around the movie.

Come on — how much conventional promotion was actually done?

The team released a teaser, not even a full trailer; there was no giant audio launch and Rajini was not sitting through endless promotional interviews.

The truth is that everyone around us wanted a little limelight simply by attaching themselves to the name RAJINI, and the hype became self-generating.

So relax and enjoy the acting treat of Rajini daaa.

The first and final fifteen minutes give hardcore mass fans some of the Superstar flavour they came for.

In between, there is a good family story narrated slowly and supported by superb performances from Rajini and Radhika.

e: Gentleman felt wonderfully refreshing after a stretch of exhausting mainstream films. The different concept kept me engaged without a single boring stretch, Mani Sharma’s background score works beautifully and the supporting cast adds value — but the complete meal is Nani, once again proving that the hero-versus-villain label matters far less than the actor inside both possibilities.
v: Simply SUPERB!!! Nani’s acting is a full meal, Mani Sharma’s BGM is terrific and I did not have a single boring moment. Hero aa? Villain aa? Forget both — NANI oka goppa ACTOR!!!!!
body:
Simply SUPERB!!!!!

Nani’s acting is FULL MEALS.

Mani Sharma’s BGM is superb too.

Special mention also goes to Srinivas Avasarala and the heroine, who both add nicely to the experience.

Personally, I did not have a single boring moment in the entire movie.

After sitting through kalaa khandalu like Sardaar Gabbar Singh, Brahmotsavam and Sarrainodu 😄, a film with a genuinely different concept felt especially refreshing.

But ultimately, Gentleman comes back to one man.

NANI hero no… villain no… kaadhu.

Oka GOPPA ACTOR!!!!!

e: Brahmotsavam triggered one of my longest rants because I could find almost nothing to defend beyond the Bala Tripuramani song and Mahesh Babu trying something slightly different there. The screenplay feels shapeless, the huge cast and lavish settings add expense rather than value, familiar emotional beats repeat without impact and the film mistakes family-value speeches for actual storytelling.
v: I apologised for commenting before watching because seeing the movie revealed the true horror 😄 No story, endless relatives, recycled Mahesh emotions and family-value lectures stretched so far that even TV serial editors might cut two hours out.
body:
CAUTION: I do not think I wrote paragraphs this long even in my B.Tech answer sheets, so read this at your own risk 😄

Before watching Brahmotsavam, a few fans told me I had no right to comment without seeing the film.

At first I thought they were merely being defensive.

After watching it, I understood their point completely.

How can you describe narakam properly without first seeing it up close? 😄

So I sincerely apologise for my earlier comments creating even the faint impression that the movie might be okay.

Now to the actual review.

Just because films like SVSC and Srimanthudu worked does not mean you can put Mahesh Babu at the centre, surround him with a lorry-load of relatives, give him the same smile and congested emotional voice, and expect audiences to keep accepting it.

I watch a Mahesh film because I know what kind of performances he has delivered in movies such as Nijam, Okkadu, Pokiri, Businessman and 1: Nenokkadine.

Here, apart from the familiar crying-tone scenes around the interval and climax, I found very little that really used the actor.

If the only argument is that Babu looks handsome, then buying a Mahesh poster and putting it in the bedroom is much cheaper than making an entire movie around that fact 😄

There are also scenes whose emotional logic simply baffled me.

When the father suddenly collapses, instead of behaving like somebody in a medical emergency the hero almost appears to ask him for one final good family-values speech.

Then comes the usual debate about responsibility.

If a film becomes a hit, everybody praises the hero’s brilliant script-selection skills.

If it becomes a disaster, suddenly only the director is responsible?

Distributors invest in a major Mahesh film because Mahesh is attached to it, so the star also has a responsibility to choose carefully.

The one thing I genuinely liked is the Bala Tripuramani song.

At least there, Mahesh tries something noticeably different.

Some people also claimed that only audiences who do not understand family values were spreading negativity about the film.

Fair enough — after watching Brahmotsavam, my brother and I, normally busy with our own lives, actually called each other to ask, “Rey, cinema chusava? Baane unnava?” 😛

So perhaps it did improve family communication after all.

Coming to the production: having money is wonderful, but spending it intelligently is even better.

Huge crowds, giant settings and more than a hundred shooting days do not automatically create a memorable family epic.

At some point somebody should have asked whether all those actors and all that scale were actually helping the story.

And Srikanth Addala — after Kotha Bangaru Lokam, I kept waiting for the writing to become tighter rather than increasingly dependent on dialect-heavy philosophical conversations without enough plot underneath them.

People outside were calling Brahmotsavam a television serial.

Please do not insult serials like that.

Even a serial editor might remove two hours from this material and use the remaining thirty minutes as an episode 😄

If you are going to make something this routine, even a straightforward mass entertainer may at least give B and C centres a reason to keep watching.

Trying to depend entirely on a so-called class audience without giving them a coherent film is much riskier.

For me, this was an exhausting lesson in how scale, stars, relatives and good intentions cannot substitute for an actual screenplay.

e: 24 stunned me because Vikram Kumar takes a complicated time-travel story and communicates it with remarkable clarity. Suriya deserves enormous credit not only for performing it but for backing such an ambitious concept as producer. The CG could be better and the romance trimmed, but those reservations barely matter beside the excitement of seeing mainstream South Indian cinema attempt something this fresh.
v: SHELL SHOCKED!!!!! How do you write something this complex and explain it as easily as peeling a banana for a child? Take a BOW, Vikram Kumar and team — and huge respect to Suriya for betting his own money and stardom on this kind of idea.
body:
SHELL SHOCKED!!!!!

How does somebody write a story this COMPLEX… and then explain it to an audience so simply?

It almost feels like peeling a banana and handing it to a small child 😄

Take a BOW, Vikram Kumar and team!!!!!

And Suriya — it takes real GUTS to accept a story like this without first worrying about all the logistical complications.

It takes even more conviction to put your own hard-earned money behind that ambition as a producer rather than merely calling yourself one because you sacrificed part of a star salary.

The CG could definitely have been better.

The romance track could also have been trimmed.

But honestly… who cares!!!!!

For Telugu-film audiences at that point, ideas and execution like this still felt wonderfully new.

That freshness, and the clarity with which such a complicated concept reaches the audience, overwhelmed the relatively small imperfections for me.

e: Oopiri balances its emotional core with enough entertainment to avoid becoming a much heavier experience. Nagarjuna nails the role, Karthi’s innocent expressions are a major asset and I loved Prakash Raj’s character. I had no issue with the remake being faithful; the team deserves credit for bringing a good French story naturally to Telugu audiences.
v: Falls just short of GREAT and lands firmly in VERY NICE territory. Nag nails it, Karthi charms, and Vamshi keeps the emotion entertaining — though I still felt something missing.
body:
Falls just short of being a GREAT movie and ends up firmly in the VERY NICE category!!!!!

Vamshi Paidipally makes sure there is enough entertainment around the emotional story; without that balance, the film could easily have become a much heavier experience in the space of Guzaarish.

Performance-wise, Nagarjuna nails it.

Karthi’s innocent expressions are a huge asset to the storyline, and I especially loved the way Prakash Raj’s character is written and performed.

I know some intellectuals will immediately start discussing how many scenes are copied directly from the French original.

WHO CARES!!!!!

We have seen enough examples where even a scene-to-scene remake gets badly messed up.

The team deserves appreciation for taking a good French story and bringing it effectively to a Telugu audience.

Not every viewer is blessed with special powers to effortlessly watch and understand French, Spanish, Romanian, Korean or English films 😄

Many of us simply enjoy experiencing a good story in our own language.

When I walked out of the theatre, I definitely had the feeling that I had watched a very nice movie.

At the same time, there was still that small feeling that… something was missing.
